title: 景泰四年福建鄉試錄
text:
第一場
四書
子張問士何如斯可謂之達矣子曰何哉爾所謂
達者子張對曰在邦必聞在家必聞子曰是聞
也非達也夫達也者質直而好義察言而觀色慮
以下人在邦必達在家必達夫聞也者色取仁而
行違居之不疑在邦必聞在家必聞
柔遠人則四方歸之懷諸侯則天下畏之
使之主祭而百神享之是天受之使之主事而事治
===
百姓安之是民受之也
易
大觀在上順而巽中正以觀天下觀盥而不薦有孚顒
若下觀而化也
有孚維心亨行有尚
初六允升大吉象曰允升大吉上合志也
夫易開物成務冒天下之道如斯而已者也是故聖人以
通天下之志以定天下之業以斷天下之疑
書
punctuated:
第一場

四書
子張問：「士何如斯可謂之達矣？」子曰：「何哉，爾所謂達者？」子張對曰：「在邦必聞，在家必聞。」子曰：「是聞也，非達也。夫達也者，質直而好義，察言而觀色，慮以下人，在邦必達，在家必達。夫聞也者，色取仁而行違，居之不疑，在邦必聞，在家必聞。」
柔遠人，則四方歸之；懷諸侯，則天下畏之。
使之主祭，而百神享之，是天受之；使之主事，而事治，百姓安之，是民受之也。

易
大觀在上，順而巽，中正以觀天下。觀，盥而不薦，有孚顒若，下觀而化也。
有孚維心亨，行有尚。
初六，允升，大吉。象曰：允升大吉，上合志也。
夫易，開物成務，冒天下之道，如斯而已者也。是故聖人以通天下之志，以定天下之業，以斷天下之疑。

書
translation_en:
First Session

Four Books
Zizhang asked: "What must a scholar-official (shi) be like before he can be called truly accomplished (da)?" The Master said: "What do you mean by what you call being accomplished?" Zizhang replied: "In a state he is sure to be renowned; in a great officer's family he is sure to be renowned." The Master said: "That is renown (wen), not accomplishment. Now the man of accomplishment is upright in his nature and loves righteousness; he examines people's words and observes their countenances, and takes thought to humble himself before others. In a state he is sure to be accomplished, and in a great officer's family he is sure to be accomplished. As for the man of renown, he assumes the outward appearance of benevolence while his actions belie it, and he dwells in this without self-doubt. In a state he is sure to be renowned, and in a great officer's family he is sure to be renowned."
By treating men from afar with gentleness, people from all four quarters will turn to him; by cherishing the feudal lords, the whole world will stand in awe of him.
When he was put in charge of sacrifices, the hundred spirits enjoyed them—this showed that Heaven accepted him. When he was put in charge of affairs, the affairs were well-governed and the common people were at peace with them—this showed that the people accepted him.

Book of Changes (Yi)
The great prospect is above; docile and penetrating, central and correct, it gives a model to look up to for all under Heaven. "Viewing (Guan): the ablution has been made, but not yet the offering; there is sincerity and an outlook of solemn dignity"—those below look toward it and are transformed.
"There is sincerity; in the heart there is unhindered progress, and action brings high reward."
Six at the beginning: Advancing with confidence; great good fortune. The Commentary on the Images (Xiang) says: "Advancing with confidence, great good fortune"—his will accords with those above.
Now the Changes opens up the resources of things, accomplishes the undertakings of men, and encompasses the Way of all under Heaven—this and nothing more. Therefore the sages used it to penetrate the wills of all under Heaven, to establish the enterprises of all under Heaven, and to resolve the doubts of all under Heaven.

Book of Documents (Shu)

title: 景泰四年福建鄉試錄
text:
先王惟時懋敬厥德克配上帝今王嗣有令緒尚監茲
哉若升高必自下若陟遐必自邇無輕民事惟難無
安厥位惟危慎終于始有言逆于汝心必求諸道
有言遜于汝志必求諸非道嗚呼弗慮胡獲弗為
胡成一人元良萬邦以貞
非天私我有商惟天佑于一德非商求于下民惟民歸
于一德德惟一動罔不吉
惠不惠懋不懋
王厥有成命治民今休
===
詩
鳲鳩在桑其子七兮淑人君子其儀一兮其儀一兮心如
結兮
勉勉我王綱紀四方
申伯信邁王餞于郿申伯還南謝于誠歸王命召伯
徹申伯土疆以峙其粻式遄其行
庸鼓有斁萬舞有奕我有嘉客亦不夷懌自古在昔
先民有作溫恭朝夕執事有恪顧予烝嘗湯孫
之將
punctuated:
先王惟時，懋敬厥德，克配上帝。今王嗣有令緒，尚監茲哉。若升高必自下，若陟遐必自邇。無輕民事，惟難；無安厥位，惟危。慎終于始。有言逆于汝心，必求諸道；有言遜于汝志，必求諸非道。嗚呼！弗慮胡獲？弗為胡成？一人元良，萬邦以貞。
非天私我有商，惟天佑于一德；非商求于下民，惟民歸于一德。德惟一，動罔不吉。
惠不惠，懋不懋。
王厥有成命，治民今休。

詩
鳲鳩在桑，其子七兮。淑人君子，其儀一兮。其儀一兮，心如結兮。
勉勉我王，綱紀四方。
申伯信邁，王餞于郿。申伯還南，謝于誠歸。王命召伯，徹申伯土疆，以峙其粻，式遄其行。
庸鼓有斁，萬舞有奕。我有嘉客，亦不夷懌。自古在昔，先民有作。溫恭朝夕，執事有恪。顧予烝嘗，湯孫之將。
translation_en:
"The former king there strove to cultivate and revere his virtue, so that he was able to be a counterpart to God on High. Now that Your Majesty has succeeded to this fine inheritance, may you take this as your mirror! It is like ascending to a height, which must begin from below; it is like traveling to a distance, which must begin from what is near. Do not treat the affairs of the people lightly, but think of their difficulty; do not feel at ease in your position, but think of its peril. Be careful of the end at the beginning. When words go against your mind, you must seek to see whether they accord with the Way; when words are agreeable to your will, you must seek to see whether they depart from the Way. Oh! Without anxious thought, what can be gained? Without action, what can be accomplished? When the One Man is supremely good, the myriad states are thereby rectified."
"It was not that Heaven showed partiality to our Shang, but that Heaven aided pure and single virtue; it was not that Shang sought the allegiance of the lower people, but that the people turned to pure and single virtue. Where virtue is pure and single, every movement is without fail auspicious."
"Be kind to the unkind; encourage those who do not strive."
"The king has received the accomplished mandate; in governing the people, there is now reposive prosperity."

Book of Odes (Shi):
"The cuckoo is in the mulberry tree, and her young ones are seven. The virtuous man, the princely one, is uniform in his deportment; uniform in his deportment, his heart is as if bound fast."
"Ever industrious is our king, bringing order and law to the four quarters."
"The Elder of Shen truly set forth, and the king gave him a farewell feast at Mei. The Elder of Shen turned south, truly going to his state at Xie. The king commanded the Elder of Shao to Tithe and lay out the lands and boundaries of the Elder of Shen, so as to store up his provisions and speed his march."
"The large bells and drums resound in harmony; the Wan dance is grandly performed. We have admirable guests, who are also pleased and delighted! From of old, in ancient times, the former men set the example: mild and reverent morning and evening, discharging their service with respect. May They look upon our winter and autumn sacrifices, offered by the descendant of Tang!"

title: 景泰四年福建鄉試錄
text:
春秋
蔡人衛人陳人從王伐鄭桓公五年齊侯宋人陳人蔡人
邾人會于北杏莊公十三年會陳人蔡人楚人鄭人盟于
齊僖公十九年
王人子突救衛莊公六年城楚丘僖公二年
齊高子來盟閔公二年楚屈完來盟于師僖公四年宋司馬
華孫來盟文公十五年
公會晉侯齊侯宋公蔡侯鄭伯衛子莒子盟于踐土僖
公二十八年同盟于亳城北襄公十一年
===
禮記
昔先王尚有德尊有道任有能舉賢而置之聚衆而誓之
是故因天事天因地事地因名山升中于天因吉土以
饗帝于郊
郊之祭也迎長日之至也大報天而主日也兆於南郊就陽
位也掃地而祭於其質也器用陶匏以象天地之性也
仁者仁此者也禮者履此者也義者宜此者也信者信此
者也強者強此者也
唯賢者能盡祭之義賢者之祭也必受其福
punctuated:
《春秋》
「蔡人、衛人、陳人從王伐鄭。」桓公五年。「齊侯、宋人、陳人、蔡人、邾人會于北杏。」莊公十三年。「會陳人、蔡人、楚人、鄭人盟于齊。」僖公十九年。
「王人子突救衛。」莊公六年。「城楚丘。」僖公二年。
「齊高子來盟。」閔公二年。「楚屈完來盟于師。」僖公四年。「宋司馬華孫來盟。」文公十五年。
「公會晉侯、齊侯、宋公、蔡侯、鄭伯、衛子、莒子盟于踐土。」僖公二十八年。「同盟于亳城北。」襄公十一年。

《禮記》
「昔先王尚有德，尊有道，任有能，舉賢而置之，聚衆而誓之。是故因天事天，因地事地，因名山升中于天，因吉土以饗帝于郊。」
「郊之祭也，迎長日之至也，大報天而主日也，兆於南郊，就陽位也。掃地而祭，於其質也。器用陶匏，以象天地之性也。」
「仁者仁此者也，禮者履此者也，義者宜此者也，信者信此者也，強者強此者也。」
「唯賢者能盡祭之義，賢者之祭也，必受其福。」
translation_en:
Spring and Autumn Annals (Chunqiu)
"Men of Cai, men of Wei, and men of Chen followed the King to attack Zheng" (5th year of Duke Huan); "The Marquis of Qi, men of Song, men of Chen, men of Cai, and men of Zhu met at Beixing" (13th year of Duke Zhuang); "[The Duke] met with men of Chen, men of Cai, men of Chu, and men of Zheng and made a covenant at Qi" (19th year of Duke Xi).
"The King's man Zitu went to the rescue of Wei" (6th year of Duke Zhuang); "They walled Chuqiu" (2nd year of Duke Xi).
"Master Gao of Qi came to make a covenant" (2nd year of Duke Min); "Qu Wan of Chu came to make a covenant with the army" (4th year of Duke Xi); "The Marshal Hua Sun of Song came to make a covenant" (15th year of Duke Wen).
"The Duke met with the Marquis of Jin, the Marquis of Qi, the Duke of Song, the Marquis of Cai, the Earl of Zheng, the Viscount of Wei, and the Viscount of Ju and made a covenant at Jiantu" (28th year of Duke Xi); "[They] made a joint covenant north of the city of Bo" (11th year of Duke Xiang).

Record of Rites (Liji)
"In antiquity, the former kings esteemed those who had virtue, honored those who possessed the Way, employed those who had ability, promoted the worthy and placed them in office, and gathered the multitude and bound them with an oath. Therefore, taking their cue from Heaven, they served Heaven; taking their cue from Earth, they served Earth; making use of famous mountains, they sent up the announcement of peace and harmony to Heaven; making use of auspicious ground, they presented offerings to the Supreme Ruler in the suburban sacrifice."
"The suburban sacrifice welcomes the arrival of the lengthening days; it is the great thanksgiving to Heaven, with the sun as its chief object. The altar is sited in the southern suburb to take the position of yang. The ground is swept and the sacrifice performed upon it, in adherence to simplicity. The vessels used are of earthenware and bottle-gourds, to symbolize the nature of Heaven and Earth."
"The benevolent person is one who practices benevolence in this; the person of ritual propriety is one who puts this into practice; the righteous person is one who acts fittingly in this; the trustworthy person is one who is trustworthy in this; the person of strength is one who exerts strength in this."
"Only the worthy person can exhaust the meaning of sacrifice; in the sacrifice of the worthy person, he will surely receive its blessings."

title: 景泰四年福建鄉試錄
text:
其流於兼愛何歟正蒙語造化則極乎日月寒暑之
變語鬼神則極乎二氣良能之妙語陰陽則一神兩
化之論備語性命則太虛氣化之論詳其與太極易
通西銘同一理歟先天圖有變象比象感象應象有
往數來數陰數陽數者何歟經世之數起乎四無非發明
此圖者也二者皆以數言其與太極之理相戾歟然理與
數固未始相離也先儒何謂太極不如先天之大先天不
如太極之精歟然先天之易先儒指為心法而後來者
反名其書為考數其言孰是孰非歟諸君子窮究理
===
數之學必貫通矣願以朱子無極之辨通書之解西銘
正蒙之訓釋皇極經世之考正會合諸子之論同出乎
一揆可也
問廉退士君子之所尚也三代而下若子雲漢之大儒猶有
求媚取容甘於美新之作昌黎一代山斗一不得志至
三上宰相之書自餘何望焉有宋盛時上以禮義維其
俗下以廉耻律其身英風義槩凛凛相望故玉堂獻
記不入翰苑河平獻頌不留蘭臺不以私書至京師則
擢之御史不以私事干朝廷則處之諫諍其人可得而
punctuated:
其流於兼愛，何歟？《正蒙》語造化，則極乎日月寒暑之變；語鬼神，則極乎二氣良能之妙；語陰陽，則一神兩化之論備；語性命，則太虛氣化之論詳。其與《太極》、《易通》、《西銘》同一理歟？《先天圖》有變象、比象、感象、應象，有往數、來數、陰數、陽數者，何歟？《經世》之數起乎四，無非發明此圖者也。二者皆以數言，其與《太極》之理相戾歟？然理與數固未始相離也。先儒何謂「《太極》不如《先天》之大，《先天》不如《太極》之精」歟？然先天之《易》，先儒指為心法，而後來者反名其書為考數，其言孰是孰非歟？諸君子窮究理數之學，必貫通矣。願以朱子《無極》之辨、《通書》之解、《西銘》《正蒙》之訓釋、《皇極經世》之考正，會合諸子之論，同出乎一揆可也。

問：廉退，士君子之所尚也。三代而下，若子雲，漢之大儒，猶有求媚取容、甘於《美新》之作；昌黎，一代山斗，一不得志，至三上宰相之書。自餘何望焉？有宋盛時，上以禮義維其俗，下以廉耻律其身，英風義槩，凛凛相望。故玉堂獻記，不入翰苑；河平獻頌，不留蘭臺。不以私書至京師，則擢之御史；不以私事干朝廷，則處之諫諍。其人可得而
translation_en:
… that it degenerates into Mozi's "universal love" (jian'ai)—why is this? When Correcting Youthful Ignorance (Zhengmeng) speaks of the creative transformations of nature, it exhausts the changes of sun and moon, cold and heat; when it speaks of ghosts and spirits, it exhausts the subtleties of the innate capacities of the two vital forces (yin and yang); when it speaks of yin and yang, the discourse on the one spirit and two transformations is complete; when it speaks of human nature and destiny, the discourse on the Supreme Vacuity (taixu) and transformation of vital force (qihua) is detailed. Does it share the same principle as the Diagram of the Supreme Ultimate (Taiji), Penetrating the Book of Changes (Yitong), and the Western Inscription (Ximing)? In the Prior-to-Heaven Diagram (Xiantiantu), there are images of change, images of comparison, images of stimulus, and images of response, as well as numbers of the past, numbers of the future, yin numbers, and yang numbers—what do these mean? The numbers in Book of Supreme World-Ordering Principles (Huangji jingshi) begin with four, and do nothing other than elucidate this diagram. Both of these speak in terms of numbers; are they at odds with the principle of the Diagram of the Supreme Ultimate? Yet principle (li) and number (shu) have never truly been separate from one another. Why did a former Confucian scholar say that "the Supreme Ultimate is not as grand as the Prior-to-Heaven, and the Prior-to-Heaven is not as subtle as the Supreme Ultimate"? Moreover, former Confucian scholars pointed to the Prior-to-Heaven Changes as a method of the mind-and-heart (xinfa), whereas later scholars conversely labeled those writings as mere investigations of numbers; whose words are right and whose are wrong? You gentlemen have thoroughly investigated the learning of principle and number, and must have achieved a comprehensive understanding of it. We hope that you will take Master Zhu's [Zhu Xi 朱熹] debates on the "Ultimateless" (Wuji), his explanations of Penetrating the Book of Changes (Tongshu), his commentaries on the Western Inscription and Correcting Youthful Ignorance, and his critical examination of the Book of Supreme World-Ordering Principles, and synthesize the discourses of these various masters to show how they all stem from a single unified principle.

Question: Modest integrity and willingness to yield are what scholar-gentlemen esteem. From the Three Dynasties downward, someone like Ziyun [Yang Xiong 楊雄], a great Confucian of the Han dynasty, still sought to flatter and ingratiate himself, willingly composing the essay "Praising the Xin Dynasty" (Meixin); and Changli [Han Yu 韓愈], the towering exemplar of an entire era, as soon as he was thwarted in his ambitions, went so far as to thrice submit letters to the Grand Councilor. What hope, then, could one have for anyone else? During the flourishing era of the Song dynasty, those above maintained customs through ritual and righteousness, while those below disciplined themselves through integrity and a sense of shame; their heroic spirit and righteous mettle stood out in awe-inspiring succession. Thus, one who presented a record of the Jade Hall was not admitted into the Hanlin Academy; one who presented a eulogy on the pacification of the Yellow River was not retained in the Imperial Library (Lantai). One who sent no private letters to the capital was promoted to Censor (yushi); one who did not petition the court over private matters was placed in a remonstrance post. Can these individuals be…

title: 景泰四年福建鄉試錄
text:
悉數歟兩及相門俱却以素定一謁大資則却以不求有安
於靜退而彦博薦之不通問訊而温公薦之其人可得
而詳陳歟方登強仕脫然勇退未及掛冠遽爾請老者
謂誰他若十年不求磨勘者有焉十五年退居者亦有
焉以至禮部第一人庭唱抗聲舊例也而不肯召試者可指其人
士第一科求試館職舊制也而不肯自陳進
歟之數子者合乎聖人之中道者誰歟可為後人，之矜
式者又誰歟千載而下亦有難免士大夫之清議者歟
諸士子為我詳陳之
===
問錢弊之利國益民其來久矣然鑄於歷山莊山小宰聽
稱責以傅別昉於何代歟又有鑄筴之錢八銖之行或
輕而三銖或重而半兩有以一當二以一當三當五十當十
大錢有折二之令當三之請又有造白鹿以為皮弊委
錢以為飛錢與夫交引之制質劑之法其輕重迭勝
當直屢更何者有便於民何者有病於下歟我
朝自國初鑄錢并前代之錢與寶鈔兼用其法甚善行之已
久然懋遷之徒往往樂於用錢而艱於用鈔雖屢禁之
未見其從其故果安在歟伊欲使鈔法流通以便民用
punctuated:
悉數歟？兩及相門，俱却以素定；一謁大資，則却以不求。有安於靜退而彦博薦之，不通問訊而温公薦之，其人可得而詳陳歟？方登強仕，脫然勇退；未及掛冠，遽爾請老者謂誰？他若十年不求磨勘者有焉，十五年退居者亦有焉。以至禮部第一人庭唱抗聲，舊例也，而不肯召試者可指其人；士第一科求試館職，舊制也，而不肯自陳進歟？之數子者，合乎聖人之中道者誰歟？可為後人之矜式者又誰歟？千載而下，亦有難免士大夫之清議者歟？諸士子為我詳陳之。
問：錢弊之利國益民，其來久矣。然鑄於歷山、莊山，小宰聽稱責以傅別，昉於何代歟？又有鑄筴之錢，八銖之行，或輕而三銖，或重而半兩；有以一當二、以一當三、當五十、當十大錢；有折二之令、當三之請；又有造白鹿以為皮弊，委錢以為飛錢，與夫交引之制、質劑之法。其輕重迭勝，當直屢更，何者有便於民？何者有病於下歟？我朝自國初鑄錢，并前代之錢與寶鈔兼用，其法甚善，行之已久。然懋遷之徒往往樂於用錢而艱於用鈔，雖屢禁之，未見其從，其故果安在歟？伊欲使鈔法流通以便民用，
translation_en:
… enumerate them all? There was one who twice approached the gate of a grand councilor, yet declined both times on the grounds that one's lot is predetermined; and another who paid a single visit to a Grand Academician of the Hall for Aid in Governance, yet declined on the grounds that he sought nothing. There was one who remained content in quiet retirement and was recommended by Wen Yanbo 文彥博, and another who sent no letters of inquiry and was recommended by Sima Guang 司馬光 (Lord Wen)—can those men be set forth in detail? Who were those who had just reached the age of forty and entered official service, yet resolutely retired in detachment, or who had not yet reached the age of hanging up their caps in retirement, yet suddenly requested leave on account of old age? As for others, there were those who for ten years did not seek a merit evaluation for promotion, and there were also those who lived in retirement for fifteen years. Furthermore, for the first-ranked candidate at the Ministry of Rites to answer in a loud voice at the court roll-call was the old precedent, yet there was one who refused [to take part in the examination or] to be summoned for a test [?]; and for a metropolitan graduate (jinshi) of the first tier to request to be tested for a historiographical or academic post (guanzhi) was the old system, yet there was one who refused to put himself forward—can these men be identified [Note: column order between these two clauses appears transposed in the transcription]? Among these several gentlemen, who conformed to the Way of the Mean of the sages? Who again may serve as a model to be emulated by posterity? And a thousand years later, are there any among them who can hardly escape the pure criticism of scholar-officials? Gentlemen, set this forth in detail for me.

Question: That coinage and currency profit the state and benefit the people is of long standing. Yet the casting of coins at Mount Li and Mount Zhuang, and the Vice Minister of State (Xiaozai) hearing cases of loans on the basis of tallied bonds (fubie)—in what eras did these originate? There were also the casting of "elm-pod" (jia) coins and the circulation of eight-zhu coins, sometimes light at three zhu and sometimes heavy at a half-ounce (banliang); there were large coins valued at one for two, one for three, one for fifty, and one for ten; there were ordinances for coins valued at two (zhe'er) and petitions for coins valued at three; and there were also the making of white deerskin into hide currency (pibi), the depositing of cash to create "flying cash" (feiqian), as well as the system of exchange vouchers (jiaoyin) and the method of commercial deeds (zhiji). As their relative weight alternated in dominance and their face values were repeatedly altered, which of them were convenient for the people, and which were harmful to those below? Since the founding of the state, our Dynasty has cast bronze coins and used both the coins of former dynasties and Precious Paper Money (baochao) together. This system is most excellent and has been practiced for a long time. Yet merchants and traders often delight in using bronze coins and are reluctant to use paper money; although this has been repeatedly prohibited, we have not seen them comply. Wherein does the reason truly lie? If one wishes to make the paper currency system circulate freely so as to be convenient for the people's use, …

title: 景泰四年福建鄉試錄
text:
何道以處之歟請著于篇以觀通濟之學
問兵戎國之大事書言詰爾戎兵張皇六師此制治保邦文
武並用之良法士君子不可以不講也周制三軍周禮六軍
軒轅五行陣風后八陣其後孫子孔明陣勢各八與李靖
之六花十二陣其目可得而悉舉歟將有三等五材五愼
五危三道二急三官三戲四機五鼓五教五習五事五法五
間五攻七政四種三術九地其詳可得而備言歟我
朝擇將用兵之法超軼前代內而衛國都外而捍疆場士氣銳而
鎧仗精伊欲盡行師之道如前所陳何陣勢可用於此
===
邊荒遠之地何機策可施於蠻海叢嶮之邦料敵制勝
隨時應機諸士子必有定見願明言之毋諉曰軍旅之事
未之學也
punctuated:
何道以處之歟？請著于篇，以觀通濟之學。

問：兵戎，國之大事。《書》言「詰爾戎兵」、「張皇六師」，此制治保邦、文武並用之良法，士君子不可以不講也。周制三軍，《周禮》六軍，軒轅五行陣，風后八陣，其後孫子、孔明陣勢各八，與李靖之六花、十二陣，其目可得而悉舉歟？將有三等、五材、五愼、五危、三道、二急、三官、三戲、四機、五鼓、五教、五習、五事、五法、五間、五攻、七政、四種、三術、九地，其詳可得而備言歟？我朝擇將用兵之法，超軼前代，內而衛國都，外而捍疆場，士氣銳而鎧仗精。伊欲盡行師之道，如前所陳，何陣勢可用於此邊荒遠之地？何機策可施於蠻海叢嶮之邦？料敵制勝，隨時應機，諸士子必有定見，願明言之，毋諉曰「軍旅之事，未之學也」。
translation_en:
…by what way should this be managed? Please set it forth in your essay, so that we may observe your learning in practical statecraft and relief of need.

Question: Military affairs are a great matter of state. The Book of Documents (Shu) speaks of "putting your weapons and armor in order" and "marshaling the Six Armies in grand array." This is a fine method for establishing order and securing the state through the joint use of civil and martial means, which scholar-gentlemen cannot fail to study. The Zhou institution of the Three Armies, the Six Armies in the Rites of Zhou (Zhouli), the Five Phases formation of Xuanyuan [the Yellow Emperor], the Eight Formations of Fenghou, and thereafter the eight formation dispositions each of Master Sun (Sunzi) and Kongming [Zhuge Liang], along with Li Jing's Six-Petal and Twelve Formations—can their specific items all be enumerated? As for generals, there are the Three Grades, Five Qualities, Five Cautions, Five Dangers, Three Ways, Two Urgencies, Three Offices, Three Games [or Tests, sanxi], Four Mechanisms, Five Drums, Five Instructions, Five Drills, Five Fundamental Factors, Five Methods, Five Kinds of Spies, Five Attacks, Seven Administrations, Four Types, Three Stratagems, and Nine Terrains—can their details be fully stated? Our Dynasty's methods of selecting generals and employing troops surpass those of former eras: internally guarding the imperial capital and externally defending the frontiers, with troop morale keen and armor and weapons refined. If we wish to exhaust the principles of conducting military campaigns as set forth above, which formation dispositions can be used in these remote borderlands, and which tactical plans can be applied in regions of barbarian seas and clustered mountain fastnesses? In assessing the enemy to achieve victory and responding to opportunities according to the moment, you gentlemen must have settled views. We wish you to state them clearly, and do not excuse yourselves by saying, "As for military affairs, I have not studied them."

title: 景泰四年福建鄉試錄
text:
邦焉內而在家而名譽有以聞於家焉子張以聞為達如是夫子得不明辨
之乎故謂夫爾之所言在邦必聞謂之聞斯可矣夫既明辨之得不詳言之乎故又謂
在家必聞謂之達則非也謂之聞斯可矣夫既明辨之得不詳言之乎故又謂
夫達也者內主忠信而所行合宜審於接物而卑以自牧此皆德脩於己而人信之
故行之於邦而無所窒礙行之於家而無所凝滯豈非達之謂乎至若聞也
者善其顏色以取於仁而行實背之又自以為是而無所忌憚此不務實而
專務求名者故謂著於邦而實德則病於己譽雖隆於家而實行則歉
於心豈非聞之謂歟噫以聞而為達此賢者所以有務外之失辨聞之非達
此聖人所以救賢者之失夫子之言不既深切而著明乎大抵子張之學病在
===
乎不務實夫子告之皆篤實之事充乎內而發乎外者也至於他日問行夫
子告以言忠信行篤敬學干禄夫子又告以言寡尤行寡悔無非所以救其失也
厥後子張有執德不弘信道不篤焉能為有無之言盖亦有得於夫子教
誨之力歟
使之主祭而百神享之是天受之使之主事而事治百姓安之是民受
之也
許評
考試官學正楊批此題似乎易而措辭實難作者不失
之泛則失之晦惟此篇破承明白講詳實
punctuated:
邦焉，內而在家，而名譽有以聞於家焉。子張以聞為達如是，夫子得不明辨之乎？故謂：夫爾之所言在邦必聞，謂之聞斯可矣；夫既明辨之，得不詳言之乎？故又謂：在家必聞，謂之達則非也，謂之聞斯可矣。夫既明辨之，得不詳言之乎？故又謂：夫達也者，內主忠信而所行合宜，審於接物而卑以自牧，此皆德脩於己而人信之，故行之於邦而無所窒礙，行之於家而無所凝滯，豈非達之謂乎？至若聞也者，善其顏色以取於仁，而行實背之，又自以為是而無所忌憚，此不務實而專務求名者，故謂著於邦而實德則病於己，譽雖隆於家而實行則歉於心，豈非聞之謂歟？噫！以聞而為達，此賢者所以有務外之失；辨聞之非達，此聖人所以救賢者之失。夫子之言，不既深切而著明乎？大抵子張之學，病在乎不務實，夫子告之，皆篤實之事，充乎內而發乎外者也。至於他日問行，夫子告以「言忠信，行篤敬」；學干禄，夫子又告以「言寡尤，行寡悔」，無非所以救其失也。厥後子張有「執德不弘，信道不篤，焉能為有無」之言，盖亦有得於夫子教誨之力歟！

使之主祭而百神享之，是天受之；使之主事而事治、百姓安之，是民受之也。
許評
考試官學正楊批：此題似乎易而措辭實難，作者不失之泛，則失之晦。惟此篇破承明白，講詳實，
translation_en:
…heard in the state, and internally within the family, his reputation is heard in the family.” Since Zizhang mistook notoriety for true distinction in this way, how could the Master not clearly distinguish between them? Therefore, he said: Regarding what you have described—being sure to be heard of in the state [and being sure to be heard of in the family, to call that true distinction is wrong; to call it notoriety is fitting. Having clearly distinguished them, how could he not explain them in detail? Therefore, he further said:]—as for true distinction, inwardly one holds fast to loyalty and trustworthiness while one’s actions accord with what is right; one is attentive in dealing with others while humbling oneself in self-cultivation. In all this, virtue is cultivated within oneself and others trust in it. Thus, when practiced in the state, there is no obstruction, and when practiced in the family, there is no stagnation—is this not what is meant by true distinction? As for notoriety, one puts on a virtuous countenance to lay claim to benevolence while one’s conduct actually violates it, and furthermore considers oneself right without any scruples. Such a person does not strive for substance, but exclusively seeks fame. Thus, although his reputation is prominent in the state, his actual virtue is defective in himself; although his praise is lofty in the family, his actual conduct leaves dissatisfaction in his heart—is this not what is meant by notoriety? Alas! Mistaking notoriety for true distinction was how this worthy fell into the error of pursuing externals; distinguishing notoriety from true distinction was how the Sage remedied the worthy’s error. Are the Master’s words not profoundly incisive and luminously clear? On the whole, the flaw in Zizhang’s learning lay in not striving for substance, and what the Master taught him were all matters of earnest substance, filled within and manifested without. Later, when he asked about conduct, the Master told him to “be loyal and trustworthy in speech, and earnest and reverent in conduct”; when he studied with a view to official emolument, the Master again told him to “speak so as to give little occasion for blame, and act so as to give little occasion for regret”—all of which was meant to remedy his shortcoming. Afterward, Zizhang uttered the words, “If a man holds to virtue without breadth, and believes in the Way without earnestness, how can he be counted as anything?”—surely this too was gained through the power of the Master’s instruction!

“When he was put in charge of sacrifices, the hundred spirits enjoyed them: this showed that Heaven accepted him. When he was put in charge of affairs, affairs were well ordered and the hundred surnames were at peace with them: this showed that the people accepted him.”
By Xu Ping.
Comment by Examiner and Confucian School Director Yang: This topic seems easy, yet phrasing it well is actually difficult; writers either err on the side of vagueness or err on the side of obscurity. Only this essay is clear in its opening and elaboration, detailed and substantive in its exposition,…

title: 景泰四年福建鄉試錄
text:
置之前列孰曰不宜
考試官教諭聶批此題明白易見而作者不詳上下文意故
多講貫不明惟此篇實而工簡而切盖深
於本領之學者況三場俱優高薦何忝
聖人祀神而神格治事而民安此可見天人之受也盖主祭而神享主事而民
安此聖人所以為天人所受也大賢即舜之行事以見天示以與之之意至矣且夫天之
為天至公無私未易得其受也今也舜之德足以典乎神天堯則薦之于天而使
之主百神之祭焉舜也達其精明之德以類上帝以禋六宗而上帝六宗莫不
洋洋左右來格而來享致其誠恪之心以望山川以徧群神而山川群神莫不
===
昭昭如在是歆而是承則神無有不享者矣夫神既享其祭則薦之於天
而天受之可知矣至若天下之事萬有不齊未易致其治也今舜之德足以
君臨天下堯則暴之于民而使治天下之事焉舜也于五典則慎徽之于百揆
度之由是五典克從而百揆時叙于四門而賓之于大麓而相之由是四門既穆
而風雨不迷則事又無不治者矣事既治矣民其有不安乎殆見黎民於變相
親相睦於四方風動之時百姓昭明相遜相順於萬國咸寧之日則民亦無有
不安焉夫事治於舜而民安於舜則暴之於民而民受之可見矣吁薦於
天而天受之則舜之有天下也乃天與之而非堯與之矣暴於民而民受之則
舜之有天下也乃人與之而非堯與之矣雖然舜之有天下豈獨堯之薦於
punctuated:
置之前列，孰曰不宜？
考試官教諭聶批：此題明白易見，而作者不詳上下文意，故多講貫不明。惟此篇實而工，簡而切，盖深於本領之學者；況三場俱優，高薦何忝？
聖人祀神而神格，治事而民安，此可見天人之受也。盖主祭而神享，主事而民安，此聖人所以為天人所受也。大賢即舜之行事，以見天示以與之之意至矣。且夫天之為天，至公無私，未易得其受也。今也舜之德足以典乎神天，堯則薦之于天，而使之主百神之祭焉。舜也達其精明之德，以類上帝，以禋六宗，而上帝、六宗莫不洋洋左右，來格而來享；致其誠恪之心，以望山川，以徧群神，而山川、群神莫不昭昭如在，是歆而是承，則神無有不享者矣。夫神既享其祭，則薦之於天而天受之，可知矣。至若天下之事，萬有不齊，未易致其治也。今舜之德足以君臨天下，堯則暴之于民，而使治天下之事焉。舜也于五典則慎徽之，于百揆度之，由是五典克從而百揆時叙；于四門而賓之，于大麓而相之，由是四門既穆而風雨不迷，則事又無不治者矣。事既治矣，民其有不安乎？殆見黎民於變，相親相睦於四方風動之時；百姓昭明，相遜相順於萬國咸寧之日，則民亦無有不安焉。夫事治於舜而民安於舜，則暴之於民而民受之，可見矣。吁！薦於天而天受之，則舜之有天下也，乃天與之，而非堯與之矣；暴於民而民受之，則舜之有天下也，乃人與之，而非堯與之矣。雖然，舜之有天下，豈獨堯之薦於…
translation_en:
…Who would say it is inappropriate to place it in the front ranks?
Examiner and Instructor Nie comments: The meaning of this topic is clear and easy to see, yet writers often fail to examine the surrounding context carefully, so their expositions lack coherence and clarity. Only this essay is substantial and skillful, concise and to the point—truly the work of a scholar deep in fundamental learning. Moreover, since his performance across all three sessions was excellent, how could a high recommendation be undeserved?
When the sage sacrifices to the spirits and the spirits arrive, and when he administers affairs and the people are at peace, one can see in this his acceptance by Heaven and humanity. Indeed, presiding over sacrifices so that the spirits enjoy them, and presiding over affairs so that the people are at peace—this is how the sage comes to be accepted by Heaven and humanity. The Great Worthy [Mencius] looked to the deeds of Shun to show how Heaven manifested its intention to give him the Empire; his explanation is most thorough. Moreover, Heaven as Heaven is utterly impartial and selfless; it is no easy thing to win its acceptance. Now, Shun's virtue was sufficient to take charge of the spirits and Heaven, so Yao presented him to Heaven and had him preside over the sacrifices to the hundred spirits. Shun extended his pure and luminous virtue to perform the *lei* sacrifice to the Supreme Ruler and the *yin* sacrifice to the Six Honored Ones, and neither the Supreme Ruler nor the Six Honored Ones failed to be vast and present as if to his left and right, coming to arrive and coming to enjoy the offerings. He devoted his sincere and reverent heart to perform the *wang* sacrifice to the mountains and rivers and to sacrifice all around to the host of spirits, and none of the mountains, rivers, or host of spirits failed to be brightly manifest as if present, delighting in and receiving the offerings; thus there were no spirits that did not enjoy them. Once the spirits enjoyed his sacrifices, it could be known that when he was presented to Heaven, Heaven accepted him. As for the affairs of the world, they are myriad and uneven; it is no easy thing to bring them to order. Now, Shun's virtue was sufficient to rule over the world as sovereign, so Yao revealed him to the people and had him govern the affairs of the world. With regard to the Five Cardinal Duties, Shun cautiously beautified them; with regard to the hundred offices, he measured and regulated them—whereupon the Five Cardinal Duties were harmoniously observed and the hundred offices were seasonally ordered. At the four gates he received the guests, and at the great foothills he oversaw the affairs—whereupon the four gates were reverent and harmonious, and amidst wind and rain he did not go astray; thus there were no affairs that were not well governed. Once affairs were well governed, how could the people not be at peace? One could see the black-haired people becoming transformed, affectionate and harmonious with one another at a time when the four quarters were moved as by the wind; the hundred surnames becoming illustrious, yielding and compliant with one another in the days when all the myriad states were at peace; thus none of the people were not at peace. Since affairs were well governed under Shun and the people were at peace under Shun, it could be seen that when he was revealed to the people, the people accepted him. Alas! Since he was presented to Heaven and Heaven accepted him, Shun's possessing the Empire was given to him by Heaven, and not given to him by Yao. Since he was revealed to the people and the people accepted him, Shun's possessing the Empire was given to him by humanity, and not given to him by Yao. Even so, how could Shun's possessing the Empire be solely a matter of Yao's presenting him to…

title: 景泰四年福建鄉試錄
text:
天暴於民而天與民受之而已觀夫避於南河之南而天下諸侯朝覲之畢歸
訟獄謳歌之咸至益以見天命人心不能舍舜而他適焉是則堯固無心於
與舜舜亦豈有心於得天下哉
易義
大觀在上順而巽中正以觀天下觀盥而不薦有孚顒若下觀而化也
李冀
同考試官教諭徐批題本正大平易作者不失之泛則失之
略此篇析理分明行文醇正宜表出之
考試官學正楊批發明彖傳之義無餘蘊矣初考取入當
===
考試官教諭聶批辭足以貫彖傳之旨義深得乎程朱
之蘊蓋用功於易學者置之高選公論歸焉
備德位之隆足以示乎下極誠敬之至有以化乎人此聖人體易而為觀也蓋聖
人為觀必本乎德位之兼隆也自非極誠敬之至又何以致其化於人哉吾夫
子以是釋觀之彖其義精矣今夫觀之為卦二陽在上四陰在下九五一爻
以陽剛之德居至尊之位為觀於上而為下所觀其為觀也大矣故以其德
而言則下坤為順上巽為巽順焉而無所乖戾巽焉而無所拂逆巽而且順
足以立軌範於天下矣五居上卦之中為得中五以陽居陽位為得正中
焉而無過不及正焉而無所偏倚中而又正足以示儀刑于四海矣然聖人
punctuated:
天、暴於民，而天與民受之而已？觀夫避於南河之南，而天下諸侯朝覲之畢歸，訟獄謳歌之咸至，益以見天命人心不能舍舜而他適焉。是則堯固無心於與舜，舜亦豈有心於得天下哉！
易義
「大觀在上，順而巽，中正以觀天下。觀，盥而不薦，有孚顒若，下觀而化也。」
李冀
同考試官教諭徐批：題本正大平易，作者不失之泛則失之略。此篇析理分明，行文醇正，宜表出之。
考試官學正楊批：發明《彖傳》之義無餘蘊矣，初考取入，當。
考試官教諭聶批：辭足以貫《彖傳》之旨，義深得乎程、朱之蘊，蓋用功於《易》學者。置之高選，公論歸焉。
備德位之隆，足以示乎下；極誠敬之至，有以化乎人。此聖人體《易》而為觀也。蓋聖人為觀，必本乎德位之兼隆也；自非極誠敬之至，又何以致其化於人哉？吾夫子以是釋《觀》之《彖》，其義精矣。今夫《觀》之為卦，二陽在上，四陰在下，九五一爻以陽剛之德，居至尊之位，為觀於上而為下所觀，其為觀也大矣。故以其德而言，則下坤為順，上巽為巽。順焉而無所乖戾，巽焉而無所拂逆，巽而且順，足以立軌範於天下矣。五居上卦之中為得中，五以陽居陽位為得正。中焉而無過不及，正焉而無所偏倚，中而又正，足以示儀刑于四海矣。然聖人
translation_en:
… Heaven and displayed him to the people, and Heaven and the people accepted him? Observe how, when he withdrew to the south of the Nan River, the feudal lords of the realm going to court audiences all turned to him, and litigants and singers of praise all came to him; by this one can see all the more that the Mandate of Heaven and the hearts of the people could not abandon Shun and go elsewhere. Thus, just as Yao certainly had no intention of giving the realm to Shun, how could Shun have had any intention of obtaining the realm!

Exposition on the Book of Changes (Yijing)

"The great manifestation is above; docile and compliant, central and correct, so as to manifest to the world. 'Viewing (Guan): the ablution has been made, but not yet the offering; there is sincerity and an aspect of solemn dignity'—those below view it and are transformed."

By Li Ji

Comment by Associate Examiner and Instructor Xu: The topic is inherently grand and straightforward, so writers either err by being too vague or err by being too sketchy. This essay analyzes the principles clearly and its style is pure and orthodox; it deserves to be singled out for praise.

Comment by Examiner and Director of Studies Yang: It elucidates the meaning of the Commentary on the Judgments (Tuanzhuan) leaving nothing unexpressed. Its selection in the initial evaluation is fitting.

Comment by Examiner and Instructor Nie: The diction suffices to penetrate the purport of the Commentary on the Judgments, and the meaning deeply grasps the profound teachings of Cheng Yi and Zhu Xi; clearly he is one who has devoted diligent effort to the study of the Changes. Placing him high among the selected candidates accords with public consensus.

Possessing the eminence of both virtue and position suffices to display a model to those below; reaching the utmost of sincerity and reverence provides the means to transform other men. This is how the sage embodies the Changes and serves as a manifestation (guan). Indeed, for the sage to serve as a manifestation to the world, it must be rooted in the combined eminence of both virtue and position; yet unless he reaches the utmost of sincerity and reverence, how could he bring about transformation among men? Our Master Confucius used this to explain the Judgment (Tuan) of the hexagram Viewing (Guan), and its meaning is subtle and precise.

Now as for Viewing as a hexagram, two yang lines are above and four yin lines are below. The single line at Nine in the Fifth place, with the virtue of yang firmness, occupies the position of supreme honor; it serves as a manifestation above and is viewed by those below, so its manifestation is great indeed. Therefore, speaking in terms of its virtue, the lower trigram Kun is docility, and the upper trigram Xun is compliance. Being docile, there is nothing perverse; being compliant, there is nothing refractory. Compliant and moreover docile, it suffices to establish a standard for the realm. The fifth line occupies the center of the upper trigram, which is attaining the mean; the fifth line, as a yang line occupying a yang position, is attaining correctness. Being central, there is neither excess nor deficiency; being correct, there is no partiality or bias. Central and moreover correct, it suffices to display a model of conduct to the Four Seas. Yet the sage…

title: 景泰四年福建鄉試錄
text:
不以德位兼隆為足尤以誠敬未至為憂故必萃精誠于一心常如始祭而盥
手之時純嚴敬于一念恒若未薦而獻腥之際而吾心之誠足以感人心之誠
將見在下之人盡其孚誠顒然仰聖人之軌範莫不相率而化成焉致其
恪敬悚然瞻聖人之儀刑莫不相觀而興起焉若舜之恭己南面而四方
風動文王之不大聲色而萬邦作孚是已大抵德位者觀示天下之本誠敬
者感化人心之要非德位之隆固無以示於人非誠敬之至又何以化乎人哉
抑觀之為卦上巽下坤而成體文王既繫其辭吾夫子於此既以卦體卦
德釋觀名義下觀而化釋卦辭矣至於下文又曰觀天之神道而四時不
忒聖人以神道設教而天下服是又極言為觀之道也吁文王之易有功
===
於伏羲而孔子之易又有功於羲文也歟
初六允升大吉象曰允升大吉上合志也
林迪
同考官教諭徐批本房作此題者固多而明實者少此
篇詞理簡當深得爻象之旨真作手也
考試官學正楊批剖析分明辭理通暢深得周孔二聖之旨
高薦奚忝
考試官教諭聶批此題作者於爻象之旨往往欠明惟此篇
詞簡潔而理精當允如初考宜在選列
punctuated:
不以德位兼隆為足，尤以誠敬未至為憂。故必萃精誠于一心，常如始祭而盥手之時；純嚴敬于一念，恒若未薦而獻腥之際，而吾心之誠足以感人心之誠。將見在下之人，盡其孚誠，顒然仰聖人之軌範，莫不相率而化成焉；致其恪敬，悚然瞻聖人之儀刑，莫不相觀而興起焉。若舜之「恭己南面」而「四方風動」，文王之「不大聲色」而「萬邦作孚」，是已。大抵德位者，觀示天下之本；誠敬者，感化人心之要。非德位之隆，固無以示於人；非誠敬之至，又何以化乎人哉？抑《觀》之為卦，上巽下坤而成體，文王既繫其辭，吾夫子於此既以卦體、卦德釋《觀》名義，「下觀而化」釋卦辭矣。至於下文又曰：「觀天之神道，而四時不忒；聖人以神道設教，而天下服。」是又極言為觀之道也。吁！文王之《易》有功於伏羲，而孔子之《易》又有功於羲、文也歟！

「初六，允升，大吉。《象》曰：允升大吉，上合志也。」
林迪
同考官教諭徐批：本房作此題者固多，而明實者少。此篇詞理簡當，深得爻、象之旨，真作手也。
考試官學正楊批：剖析分明，辭理通暢，深得周、孔二聖之旨，高薦奚忝？
考試官教諭聶批：此題作者於爻、象之旨往往欠明，惟此篇詞簡潔而理精當，允如初考，宜在選列。
translation_en:
…does not consider the dual eminence of virtue and position to be sufficient, and worries even more that his sincerity and reverence have not reached their utmost. Therefore, he must concentrate pure sincerity in a single mind, always as if at the moment of washing the hands at the beginning of a sacrifice; and he must keep strict reverence pure in a single thought, constantly as if at the occasion of offering raw flesh before the main presentation. Thus, the sincerity of his own mind is sufficient to move the sincerity of people's minds. We shall see that those below, exhausting their trustful sincerity and looking up in solemn admiration at the sage's standard, will without exception follow one another and be transformed; extending their respectful reverence and gazing in awe upon the sage's model, they will without exception observe one another and be inspired to rise up. Such were Shun's "making himself reverent and facing south" while "the four quarters were moved as by the wind," and King Wen's "not making a great display of sound or color" while "the myriad states placed their trust in him." In general, virtue and position are the foundation for displaying oneself to the world, while sincerity and reverence are the essential means for moving and transforming human hearts. Without the eminence of virtue and position, there is truly nothing with which to display oneself to others; yet without the utmost sincerity and reverence, how could one transform others? Furthermore, as for the hexagram Guan (Contemplation), its form is composed of Xun above and Kun below. After King Wen appended his judgment to it, our Master [Confucius] here explained the meaning of the name Guan in terms of the hexagram's form and virtues, and explained the hexagram statement with the phrase "those below contemplate him and are transformed." Coming to the text below, he further said: "Contemplating the mysterious way of Heaven, the four seasons do not err; the sage establishes his teachings in accordance with the mysterious way, and all under Heaven submit." This, again, is to speak to the utmost of the way of serving as an exemplar for contemplation. Ah! Did not the Changes (Yi) of King Wen render service to Fuxi, and the Changes of Confucius in turn render service to Fuxi and King Wen?

"First Six: Advancing upward with confidence, great good fortune. The Commentary on the Images (Xiang) says: 'Advancing upward with confidence, great good fortune'—he is in accord with the will of those above."
Lin Di 林迪
Comment by Associate Examiner and Instructor Xu: Many in this examination ward wrote on this topic, yet few were clear and substantive. In this essay, the words and principles are concise and fitting, deeply grasping the purport of the line statement and the Commentary on the Images. He is truly a master hand.
Comment by Examiner and Director of Studies Yang: The analysis is clear and distinct, the words and principles fluent and coherent. It deeply grasps the purport of the two sages, the Duke of Zhou and Confucius. How could a high recommendation be undeserved?
Comment by Examiner and Instructor Nie: Writers on this topic often lack clarity regarding the purport of the line statement and the Commentary on the Images. Only this essay is concise and clean in diction and precise and fitting in principle. It truly matches the initial evaluation and ought to be placed among the selected candidates.

title: 景泰四年福建鄉試錄
text:
陰信陽而上進爻旣著其占之吉象復申其志之同盖陰非從陽不能以
自升也今升之初六旣信從於陽而與之同升則能升而獲吉矣爻象
聖人得不著其占之吉于前而申其志之同于後哉且夫升之初六居巽之
下上無應援當升之時柔不能以自升故信於九二之陽而九二亦信之以
同升焉處下卦之初弱不能以自進惟從於九二之剛而九二亦允之以偕
進焉升不徒升升則遂夫揚于王庭之願矣非若姤之繫于金柅也吉
孰大焉進不徒進進則遂夫共惟帝臣之心矣非若屯之乘馬班如也
善孰過焉夫周公係爻著占其義如此吾夫子於小象復申言之以為
初六之所以允升而大吉者由其與上合志也上謂九二合志者志无不同
===
也上有南征之心初六亦有南征之心上與初六位雖有高下之殊而
其心則相與昭合而無間二有作賓之志初六亦有作賓之志初六與二質
雖有剛柔之異而其志則相與交孚而為一聲應氣求初之心即上之心
鶴鳴子和二之志即初之志夫如是則其獲乎大吉也宜哉抑論上坤下
巽伏羲名升之卦也元亨用見大人勿恤南征吉文王彖升之辭也至於
初六周公則以允升大吉著其爻孔子復以上合志也由其象無非發明卦
爻所以為升之義也吁羲文周孔同此心也畫卦繫辭同此理也孰
謂文王之易非伏羲之易而周孔之易非羲文之易也歟
書義
punctuated:
陰信陽而上進，爻旣著其占之吉，象復申其志之同。盖陰非從陽，不能以自升也。今升之初六，旣信從於陽而與之同升，則能升而獲吉矣。爻、象聖人，得不著其占之吉于前，而申其志之同于後哉？且夫升之初六，居巽之下，上無應援。當升之時，柔不能以自升，故信於九二之陽，而九二亦信之以同升焉；處下卦之初，弱不能以自進，惟從於九二之剛，而九二亦允之以偕進焉。升不徒升，升則遂夫「揚于王庭」之願矣，非若《姤》之「繫于金柅」也，吉孰大焉？進不徒進，進則遂夫「共惟帝臣」之心矣，非若《屯》之「乘馬班如」也，善孰過焉？夫周公係爻著占，其義如此。吾夫子於《小象》復申言之，以為初六之所以「允升」而「大吉」者，由其與「上合志」也。上謂九二，合志者，志无不同也。上有「南征」之心，初六亦有「南征」之心，上與初六，位雖有高下之殊，而其心則相與昭合而無間；二有作賓之志，初六亦有作賓之志，初六與二，質雖有剛柔之異，而其志則相與交孚而為一。聲應氣求，初之心即上之心；鶴鳴子和，二之志即初之志。夫如是，則其獲乎大吉也，宜哉！抑論上坤下巽，伏羲名《升》之卦也；「元亨，用見大人，勿恤，南征吉」，文王彖《升》之辭也。至於初六，周公則以「允升，大吉」著其爻，孔子復以「上合志也」由其象，無非發明卦爻所以為升之義也。吁！羲、文、周、孔，同此心也；畫卦、繫辭，同此理也。孰謂文王之《易》非伏羲之《易》，而周、孔之《易》非羲、文之《易》也歟？

書義
translation_en:
When yin places its trust in yang and advances upward, the line statement first sets forth the auspiciousness of its prognostication, and the Commentary on the Images then further explains the commonality of their aspirations. For unless yin follows yang, it is unable to ascend on its own. Now, since Six at the Beginning in the hexagram Ascending (Sheng) trusts and follows yang and ascends together with it, it is able to ascend and obtain good fortune. How could the sages who composed the line statement and the Commentary on the Images fail to set forth the auspiciousness of its prognostication beforehand and reiterate the commonality of their aspirations afterward?

Moreover, Six at the Beginning of Ascending dwells at the bottom of the trigram Xun (Wind/Wood) and has no corresponding supporter above. At the time of Ascending, being yielding, it cannot ascend by itself; therefore, it places its trust in the yang of Nine in the Second Place, and Nine in the Second Place likewise trusts it so that they ascend together. Dwelling at the beginning of the lower trigram, being weak, it cannot advance by itself; it simply follows the firmness of Nine in the Second Place, and Nine in the Second Place likewise gives its assent so that they advance in tandem. Its ascending is not a mere ascending: in ascending, it fulfills the wish of "being proclaimed in the king's court," unlike the case in Coming to Meet (Gou) of being "tied to a metal brake"—what good fortune could be greater than this? Its advancing is not a mere advancing: in advancing, it fulfills the mind of "serving together as ministers of the sovereign," unlike the case in Difficulty at the Beginning (Zhun) of "mounted on horses, yet pacing back and forth"—what goodness could surpass this?

Such is the meaning of the Duke of Zhou's appending the line statement and setting forth the prognostication. Our Master [Confucius], in the Lesser Images (Xiaoxiang), further elaborated on it, holding that the reason Six at the Beginning "ascends with confidence" and has "great good fortune" is that it "shares the aspiration of the one above." "The one above" refers to Nine in the Second Place; "sharing the aspiration" means that their aspirations are in no way different. The one above has a mind set on "advancing southward," and Six at the Beginning likewise has a mind set on "advancing southward." Although the one above and Six at the Beginning differ in the height of their positions, their minds are in bright harmony without any gap between them. The Second has the aspiration of being a guest of the king, and Six at the Beginning likewise has the aspiration of being a guest of the king. Although Six at the Beginning and the Second differ in their yielding and firm natures, their aspirations trustingly intersect and become one. Like sounds echoing one another and vital energies seeking one another, the mind of the Beginning is none other than the mind of the one above; like a crane calling out and its young answering, the aspiration of the Second is none other than the aspiration of the Beginning. Since it is like this, is it not fitting that it obtains great good fortune!

Furthermore, if we consider the hexagram as a whole: with the trigram Kun above and Xun below, Fuxi named it the hexagram Ascending; "Supreme success; it is fitting to see the great man; do not worry; advancing southward brings good fortune"—these are the words of King Wen's Judgment (Tuan) on Ascending. Coming to Six at the Beginning, the Duke of Zhou manifested its line with the words "Ascending with confidence, great good fortune," and Confucius further drew out [?; 由, likely a misprint for 申] its Image with the words "It shares the aspiration of the one above"—all of which are nothing other than elucidations of the principle whereby the hexagram and its lines constitute Ascending. Ah! Fuxi, King Wen, the Duke of Zhou, and Confucius all shared this same mind; drawing the hexagrams and appending the statements both embody this same principle. Who would say that the Changes (Yi) of King Wen is not the Changes of Fuxi, or that the Changes of the Duke of Zhou and Confucius is not the Changes of Fuxi and King Wen?

Expositions on the Book of Documents (Shu yi)

title: 景泰四年福建鄉試錄
text:
作於悔過之初深自喜慰故其辭温此篇作於改過之後慮其或不克終
故其辭深以厲可謂善於告君者矣厥後太甲克終厥德非伊尹訓
迪之力而疇歟
王厥有成命治民今休
許評
同考試官教諭鮑批題意雖平易而講貫潔要者鮮此
篇理有發明詞無冗泛非熟於經者不
能也
考試官學正楊批辭達意周發明期望宅洛之效殆無
===
餘蘊誠佳作也
考試官教諭聶批書經二百餘卷作者固多此篇尤簡
潔有理誠銕中之錚錚者
天命固於上治化美於下此大臣期君治洛之效也盖洛邑之作繋於天
人大矣人君能紹上帝服土中則天命之固治化之美有不期而然者矣
召公舉周公之言以告成王其意不旣深乎且夫洛為天地之中人君所
以凝天命者在此今王而宅天下之中紹上帝之治將見天監厥德用
集大命保佑命之自天中之眷顧之已隆者愈隆而弗替付托之已重
者益重而無窮鞏基圖于於萬斯年之永者豈基圖之永乎寔天
punctuated:
作於悔過之初，深自喜慰，故其辭温；此篇作於改過之後，慮其或不克終，故其辭深以厲，可謂善於告君者矣。厥後太甲克終厥德，非伊尹訓迪之力而疇歟？

「王厥有成命，治民今休。」
許評。
同考試官教諭鮑批：題意雖平易，而講貫潔要者鮮。此篇理有發明，詞無冗泛，非熟於經者不能也。
考試官學正楊批：辭達意周，發明期望宅洛之效，殆無餘蘊，誠佳作也。
考試官教諭聶批：《書經》二百餘卷，作者固多，此篇尤簡潔有理，誠銕中之錚錚者。

天命固於上，治化美於下，此大臣期君治洛之效也。盖洛邑之作，繋於天人大矣。人君能紹上帝、服土中，則天命之固、治化之美，有不期而然者矣。召公舉周公之言以告成王，其意不旣深乎？且夫洛為天地之中，人君所以凝天命者在此。今王而宅天下之中，紹上帝之治，將見天監厥德，用集大命；保佑命之，自天中之。眷顧之已隆者，愈隆而弗替；付托之已重者，益重而無窮。鞏基圖于「於萬斯年」之永者，豈基圖之永乎？寔天
translation_en:
…was composed at the beginning of his repentance, when [Yi Yin 伊尹] was deeply pleased and comforted, so its words are gentle; this chapter was composed after he had mended his ways, out of concern that he might not be able to persevere to the end, so its words are profound and stern. He may truly be called skillful at admonishing his ruler! That Tai Jia 太甲 was afterward able to maintain his virtue to the end—to whom else was this due if not to the strength of Yi Yin's instruction and guidance?

"The King will have an established Mandate, and his governance of the people will now be auspicious." [Book of Documents (Shujing), "Announcement of Shao" (Shaogao 召誥)]
By Xu Ping 許評.
Comment by Associate Examiner County Director of Studies (jiaoyu) Bao 鮑: Although the meaning of the topic is plain and straightforward, few expound it with conciseness and precision. This essay elucidates the principles and has no verbose or superficial phrasing; none but one thoroughly versed in the Classic could have produced it.
Comment by Examiner Subprefectural Director of Studies (xuezheng) Yang 楊: The language is expressive and the thought comprehensive. It elucidates the anticipated effects of taking up residence at Luo 洛 until almost nothing is left unexpressed—truly a fine piece of work.
Comment by Examiner County Director of Studies Nie 聶: Among more than two hundred papers on the Book of Documents (Shujing), there are certainly many capable writers, yet this essay is especially concise and well-reasoned—truly the finest clanging metal among iron.

When the Mandate of Heaven is secured above and transformative governance is perfected below—this is the effect the great minister anticipated from his ruler's governing at Luo. Indeed, the building of the city of Luo was of great consequence to both Heaven and humankind. If a ruler is able to succeed the Supreme Lord on High and govern in the center of the land, then the security of Heaven's Mandate and the perfection of transformative governance will come about even without being sought. When the Duke of Shao (Shao Gong 召公) cited the words of the Duke of Zhou (Zhou Gong 周公) to admonish King Cheng 成王, was his intention not profound indeed? Moreover, Luo is the center of Heaven and Earth, and it is here that the ruler consolidates the Mandate of Heaven. Now, if the King dwells at the center of All under Heaven and succeeds to the governance of the Supreme Lord on High, we shall see that Heaven inspects his virtue and thereby concentrates the Great Mandate upon him; protecting, aiding, and gevening him the charge, from Heaven it renews it [?; reading 中 for 申]. The favor that is already abundant will become ever more abundant without ceasing; the trust that is already weighty will grow ever weightier without end. Securing the dynastic foundation for the perpetuity of "ten thousand years"—is this merely the perpetuity of the foundation? In truth, it is the Mandate of Heaven…

title: 景泰四年福建鄉試錄
text:
命之永一成而不變耳奠國祚於萬有千歲之久者豈國祚之久歟實
帝命之久一定而不易耳王者之有天成命如此何莫非紹上帝之所致
乎洛為四方都會之所人君所以固人心者在是今王中天下而立定四海
之民殆見禮樂教化之昭明有以措斯世於平康綱紀文章之宣布有
以致萬方之化服父子兄弟各止其所而黎民有於変之休所謂五
品不遜者無有也農工商賈各安其業而下民有祗台之美所謂一夫不獲
者無有也王者治民今休如此何莫而非服土中之所致歟抑考洛邑既
成成王始政召公因周公之歸作書以告成王上文既以紹上帝服土中為言
而此又舉周公之語以告之以見作洛所以配上帝奉祭祀凝天命成治功
===
其重如此盖下文將自進其敬德祈天之言必先引周公之語以啓其端
也召公之忠愛何其至歟
詩義
申伯信邁王餞于郿申伯還南謝于誠歸王命召伯徹申伯土疆以
峙其粻式遄其行
周瑛
同考試官教諭羅批詩經近三百卷作者多為此題所窘
惟此篇寫出宣王愛舅之情吉甫贈言
之美正合題意而且文辭豐潤誠所眷竚
punctuated:
命之永，一成而不變耳；奠國祚於萬有千歲之久者，豈國祚之久歟？實帝命之久，一定而不易耳。王者之有天成命如此，何莫非紹上帝之所致乎？洛為四方都會之所，人君所以固人心者在是。今王中天下而立，定四海之民，殆見禮樂教化之昭明，有以措斯世於平康；綱紀文章之宣布，有以致萬方之化服。父子兄弟各止其所，而黎民有「於変」之休，所謂「五品不遜」者，無有也；農工商賈各安其業，而下民有「祗台」之美，所謂「一夫不獲」者，無有也。王者治民今休如此，何莫而非服土中之所致歟？抑考洛邑既成，成王始政，召公因周公之歸，作書以告成王。上文既以「紹上帝」、「服土中」為言，而此又舉周公之語以告之，以見作洛所以配上帝、奉祭祀、凝天命、成治功，其重如此。盖下文將自進其敬德祈天之言，必先引周公之語以啓其端也。召公之忠愛，何其至歟！

詩義
「申伯信邁，王餞于郿。申伯還南，謝于誠歸。王命召伯，徹申伯土疆，以峙其粻，式遄其行。」
周瑛
同考試官教諭羅批：《詩經》近三百卷，作者多為此題所窘。惟此篇寫出宣王愛舅之情、吉甫贈言之美，正合題意，而且文辭豐潤，誠所眷竚…
translation_en:
…Heaven's Mandate that is once established and never changes; and establishing the dynastic fortune for ten thousand and a thousand years—is it merely the longevity of the dynastic fortune? In truth, it is the longevity of the Sovereign on High's Mandate, once fixed and never altered! That the true king possesses the accomplished Mandate of Heaven in such a manner—how could any of this not be brought about by continuing the work of the Sovereign on High?

Luo is the metropolis where the four quarters converge, and it is here that the ruler consolidates the hearts of the people. Now, when the king stands in the center of the realm and settles the people within the four seas, one will surely see the brilliance of rites, music, instruction, and transformation, sufficient to place this world in peace and tranquility; and the promulgation of moral mainstays, laws, and cultural institutions, sufficient to bring the myriad regions into transformed submission. Fathers, sons, elder brothers, and younger brothers will each rest in their proper place, and the black-haired people will enjoy the blessing of "Oh! how transformed!", so that what is called "the five categories of relationships being uncompliant" will not exist. Farmers, artisans, and merchants will each be content in their occupations, and the common people will possess the virtue of "reverently following me," so that what is called "a single man failing to find his place" will not exist. That the true king governs the people and achieves present blessings in such a manner—how could any of this not be brought about by governing from the center of the land?

Moreover, if we examine the matter: after the city of Luo had been completed and King Cheng assumed personal rule, the Duke of Shao, on the occasion of the Duke of Zhou's return, composed this document to instruct King Cheng. Above, he had already spoken of "continuing the work of the Sovereign on High" and "governing from the center of the land," and here he again cites the words of the Duke of Zhou to instruct him, so as to show that the building of Luo was the means to match the Sovereign on High, uphold the sacrifices, consolidate Heaven's Mandate, and accomplish the work of governance—so great was its importance! For in the text below, as he is about to present his own words on revering virtue and praying to Heaven, he must first quote the words of the Duke of Zhou to open the way. How supreme indeed was the loyal affection of the Duke of Shao!

Exposition on the Classic of Odes (Shijing)

"The Earl of Shen truly set forth; the king gave him a farewell feast at Mei. The Earl of Shen turned south, truly going to return to Xie. The king commanded the Earl of Shao to lay out the Earl of Shen's lands and boundaries, to store up his dry provisions, and thus to speed his journey."

By Zhou Ying 周瑛

Comment by Associate Examiner Instructor Luo: Among the nearly three hundred scripts on the Classic of Odes, most writers were stymied by this topic. Only this essay captures King Xuan's affection for his maternal uncle and the beauty of Yin Jifu's parting words, matching the meaning of the topic while also being rich and lustrous in its diction. Truly, it is one that we regard with fond expectation [?]…

title: 景泰四年福建鄉試錄
text:
瀟林者也宜冠本經
考試官學正楊批吟咏性情作者鮮得惟此篇簡而明
文而實形容詩人詠賢君待臣之意宛然
在目蓋深得葩經之旨者也
考試官教諭聶批此題作者多於信邁誠歸処失其本
旨惟此篇辭旨有法文采燁然讀之三復三嘆
觀王者因親臣之歸國旣致餞而有以果其行當觀王者命大臣之治土
復致備而有以速其行蓋王者於親臣之出封不惟致餞而欲其行之果而
又致備以資其行之速則其待親臣之厚為何如哉昔者申伯出封于
===
謝尹吉甫作詩送之謂夫申伯為王之元舅析圭儋爵非一日而未得果
於行也膏車秣馬非一朝而未得遂其往也今也申伯信為邁矣王在
岐周可不往餞于郿而送之乎吾知肆筵設席而禮意之甚隆路車乘
黃而贈賵之甚厚其致餞也為何如王者旣致餞矣則伯申之行豈有不
果者乎吾知四牡業業而載馳載驅於南方之道徒御嘽嘽而將翔於謝
邑之郊向也行有未果今則信於行矣向也歸有未遂今則誠於歸矣然
使道路儲蓄之不備又豈無淹留之患哉故王命召伯不徒命也于以徹
申伯之土而使土地之適均于以徹申伯之疆而俾疆界之是正將見什一之征
有以充道路之委積賦稅之犬入有以峙廬市之餱糧夫然後今日之五
punctuated:
瀟林者也，宜冠本經。
考試官學正楊批：吟咏性情，作者鮮得。惟此篇簡而明，文而實，形容詩人詠賢君待臣之意，宛然在目，蓋深得《葩經》之旨者也。
考試官教諭聶批：此題作者多於「信邁」、「誠歸」処失其本旨，惟此篇辭旨有法，文采燁然，讀之三復三嘆。
觀王者因親臣之歸國，旣致餞而有以果其行；當觀王者命大臣之治土，復致備而有以速其行。蓋王者於親臣之出封，不惟致餞而欲其行之果，而又致備以資其行之速，則其待親臣之厚為何如哉！昔者申伯出封于謝，尹吉甫作詩送之，謂夫申伯為王之元舅，析圭儋爵非一日，而未得果於行也；膏車秣馬非一朝，而未得遂其往也。今也申伯信為邁矣，王在岐周，可不往餞于郿而送之乎？吾知肆筵設席而禮意之甚隆，路車乘黃而贈賵之甚厚，其致餞也為何如！王者旣致餞矣，則伯申之行，豈有不果者乎？吾知四牡業業，而載馳載驅於南方之道；徒御嘽嘽，而將翔於謝邑之郊。向也行有未果，今則信於行矣；向也歸有未遂，今則誠於歸矣。然使道路儲蓄之不備，又豈無淹留之患哉？故王命召伯，不徒命也，于以徹申伯之土，而使土地之適均；于以徹申伯之疆，而俾疆界之是正。將見什一之征，有以充道路之委積；賦稅之犬入，有以峙廬市之餱糧。夫然後今日之五
translation_en:
…in the grove of letters [瀟林?]; it ought to be placed first in this Classic.

Examiner Yang, Director of Studies (學正), comments: Few writers manage to capture the chanting of human nature and emotions. Only this essay is concise yet clear, refined yet substantial. It vividly portrays the poet's intent in singing of how a worthy ruler treats his minister, making it appear right before one's eyes. Indeed, he has deeply grasped the purport of the Classic of Poetry (Pajing).

Examiner Nie, Instructor (教諭), comments: On this topic, most writers missed the original meaning at the phrases "truly sets forth" (xin mai) and "sincerely returns" (cheng gui). Only this essay is methodical in its diction and purport, and brilliant in its literary grace; reading it makes one recite it thrice and sigh in admiration thrice over.

When we observe how the true king, on account of an intimate minister returning to his state, held a farewell banquet and thereby brought his departure to fruition, we ought also to observe how the true king commanded a great minister to regulate the lands, further making preparations and thereby hastening his journey. For when an intimate minister goes out to his fief, the true king not only holds a farewell banquet wishing to bring his departure to fruition, but also makes preparations to facilitate the speed of his journey—how generous indeed is his treatment of his intimate minister!

In antiquity, when the Earl of Shen (Shen Bo) went out to be enfeoffed at Xie, Yin Jifu composed a poem to see him off. He meant to say that the Earl of Shen, as the King's eldest maternal uncle, had been granted a jade tablet and borne a noble rank for more than a single day, yet had not been able to bring his departure to fruition; he had greased his carriage wheels and fed his horses grain for more than a single morning, yet had not been able to fulfill his journey. Now, the Earl of Shen is truly setting forth! With the King at Qizhou, how could he not go to give him a farewell banquet at Mei and see him off? I know that mats and seats were spread out with the utmost ceremonial courtesy, and a state carriage and team of four bay horses were presented as most generous parting gifts [贈賵, lit. funeral gifts, used here for parting gifts]—how grand was that farewell banquet! Once the King had held the farewell banquet, how could the departure of the Earl of Shen [written 伯申] not be brought to fruition? I know that his four stallions were strong and stalwart as he galloped and drove along the southern road, and his footmen and charioteers were numerous and at ease as they were about to soar into the suburbs of the city of Xie. Previously, his departure had not been brought to fruition, but now he truly sets forth on his journey; previously, his return had not been fulfilled, but now he sincerely returns.

Yet if the stores and provisions along the road were not prepared, how could there be no worry of delay and lingering? Therefore, when the King commanded the Earl of Shao (Shao Bo), it was not an empty command: he went to tax-apportion (che) the lands of the Earl of Shen so as to make the land allotments properly equalized, and he went to tax-apportion the boundaries of the Earl of Shen so as to make the borders rectified. One would then see that theone-tenth levy sufficed to fill the stores accumulated along the roads, and the great [犬, error for 大] revenue from taxes sufficed to lay up dry provisions at the way-stations and markets. Only after this could today's fifty…

title: 景泰四年福建鄉試錄
text:
十里而今日之行無所留明日之五十里而明日之行無所滯其行之速
為何如哉宣王之待元舅其恩意之周浹綜理之微密如此詩人形諸咏
歌不亦宜乎抑考申伯之於周其生也有所自其出也有所為觀其所謂
維嶽降神生甫及申則申伯之生既鍾嶽神之秀矣所謂四國于蕃四
方于宣則申伯之出又足以為王國之翰矣宣王得大臣之賢而致中興
之盛豈不於斯而可見乎
庸鼓有斁萬舞有奕我有嘉客亦不夷懌自古在昔先民有作
溫恭朝夕執事有恪顧予烝嘗湯孫之將
吳繹思
===
同考試官教諭羅批此篇前言祭之始此言祭之終場中作者
皆不能分析題意又於自古在昔先民處不
能發明惟此得之允宜表出
考試官學正楊批形容商人盡樂與敬之實而致仰先王
來享之意洋洋盈耳誠可羨也
考試官教諭聶批美盛德告成功藹然當時之氣象作
者固如是夫
樂足以感先代之後敬足以紹先世之傳此後王所以冀先王之享祭也夫宗
廟之祭固尚夫樂而尤本乎敬也今也樂之盛既足以感乎人敬之行又
punctuated:
十里，而今日之行無所留；明日之五十里，而明日之行無所滯。其行之速為何如哉！宣王之待元舅，其恩意之周浹、綜理之微密如此，詩人形諸咏歌，不亦宜乎！抑考申伯之於周，其生也有所自，其出也有所為。觀其所謂「維嶽降神，生甫及申」，則申伯之生，既鍾嶽神之秀矣；所謂「四國于蕃，四方于宣」，則申伯之出，又足以為王國之翰矣。宣王得大臣之賢，而致中興之盛，豈不於斯而可見乎！

「庸鼓有斁，萬舞有奕。我有嘉客，亦不夷懌。自古在昔，先民有作。溫恭朝夕，執事有恪。顧予烝嘗，湯孫之將。」
吳繹思〔同考試官教諭羅批：此篇前言祭之始，此言祭之終。場中作者皆不能分析題意，又於「自古在昔，先民」處不能發明，惟此得之，允宜表出。考試官學正楊批：形容商人盡樂與敬之實，而致仰先王來享之意，洋洋盈耳，誠可羨也。考試官教諭聶批：美盛德，告成功，藹然當時之氣象。作者固如是夫！〕

樂足以感先代之後，敬足以紹先世之傳，此後王所以冀先王之享祭也。夫宗廟之祭，固尚夫樂，而尤本乎敬也。今也，樂之盛既足以感乎人，敬之行又
translation_en:
…fifty li today, and today's march meets no delay; fifty li tomorrow, and tomorrow's march suffers no hindrance. How swift is his journey! In treating his elder maternal uncle, King Xuan's grace and affection were so thorough and his arrangements so meticulous; was it not fitting that the poet gave voice to this in song? Moreover, if we examine the Earl of Shen's relation to the Zhou, his birth had its origin, and his going forth into service had its purpose. Looking at the lines, "The lofty mountains sent down a spirit, giving birth to Fu and Shen," the Earl of Shen's birth was already endowed with the finest essence of the mountain spirit; and in the lines, "A screen to the four states, diffusing virtue to the four quarters," the Earl of Shen's going forth was furthermore sufficient to serve as a bulwark for the royal domain. That King Xuan obtained the worthiness of great ministers and brought about the flourishing of his restoration—can it not be seen right here?

"The large bells and drums ring out abundantly; the myriad dances are grandly arrayed. I have admirable guests, who also are delighted and pleased. From antiquity, in times of old, the former people established this: mild and reverent morning and night, performing the service with care. Look with favor upon my winter and autumn sacrifices, offered by the descendant of Tang."
By Wu Yisi 吳繹思. [Comment by Associate Examiner Instructor Luo 羅: Earlier in this ode it speaks of the beginning of the sacrifice; here it speaks of the conclusion of the sacrifice. None of the candidates in the examination hall were able to analyze the meaning of the topic, nor could they elucidate the passage "From antiquity, in times of old, the former people." Only this essay grasped it and truly deserves to be singled out for publication. Comment by Examiner Director of Studies Yang 楊: It depicts the reality of the Shang people's utmost music and reverence, conveying their hope that the former kings would come to enjoy the offering. It fills the ears in rich abundance and is truly admirable. Comment by Examiner Instructor Nie 聶: Praising flourishing virtue and announcing successful accomplishment, it exudes the genial atmosphere of that era. The author has truly achieved this!]

When music is sufficient to move the descendants of former dynasties, and reverence is sufficient to continue the transmission from former generations, this is whereby a later king hopes that the former kings will enjoy the sacrifice. Now, sacrifices in the ancestral temple certainly esteem music, yet they are even more fundamentally rooted in reverence. Here, the grandeur of the music is already sufficient to move men, and the practice of reverence furthermore…

title: 景泰四年福建鄉試錄
text:
有以傳於古宜乎商人兾先王之眷顧焉是詩祀成湯之樂也且夫金屬
曰庸革屬曰鼓而謂之有斁則疾徐有節清濁相宣斁斁然其盛矣
羽籥曰文干戚曰舞萬舞而謂之有奕則綴兆可觀儀文不紊奕奕
然有序矣樂舞之盛如此是以先代之後助祭之賓聞鐘鼓之音莫
不欣然而有和樂之意覩萬舞之容莫不怡然而有喜悅之心則樂之
感乎人者為何如哉然樂既感乎人而敬豈不傳於古乎且不徒曰自古
而必曰在昔則此敬之行非一人矣不徒曰在昔而必曰先民則是敬之行
非一日矣古人朝夕必溫恭也吾則溫恭於朝夕之間無一時之或怠焉古
人執事必有恪也吾則恪敬於執事之際無一事之敢慢焉其敬之法於
===
古人者又何如哉夫樂既盛矣敬既至矣固是以感格先王之神矣而
湯孫之心尤不敢以是而自足也謂夫成湯於冥冥之中其庶幾顧
我冬烝之祭乎是祭也乃湯孫所親奉而非攝以他人也烈祖於昭
昭之際其庶幾顧我秋嘗之祀乎是祀也乃湯孫所躬主而非委之於
他職也拳拳焉致其丁寧之意懇懇焉兾其眷顧之深先王有不來
格乎抑是詩商人祀成湯而作也然有樂焉必有禮有禮焉必有樂其
所謂庸鼓有斁萬舞有奕則樂之和為可知所謂溫恭朝夕執事
有恪則禮之謹為可見樂本於和禮本於敬此商人之禮樂所以為盛
也歟此其所以美盛德而告成功也歟
punctuated: 有以傳於古，宜乎商人兾先王之眷顧焉。是詩祀成湯之樂也。且夫金屬曰「庸」，革屬曰「鼓」，而謂之「有斁」，則疾徐有節，清濁相宣，斁斁然其盛矣；羽籥曰「文」，干戚曰「舞」，萬舞而謂之「有奕」，則綴兆可觀，儀文不紊，奕奕然有序矣。樂舞之盛如此，是以先代之後、助祭之賓，聞鐘鼓之音，莫不欣然而有和樂之意；覩萬舞之容，莫不怡然而有喜悅之心。則樂之感乎人者為何如哉！然樂既感乎人，而敬豈不傳於古乎？且不徒曰「自古」而必曰「在昔」，則此敬之行非一人矣；不徒曰「在昔」而必曰「先民」，則是敬之行非一日矣。古人朝夕必溫恭也，吾則溫恭於朝夕之間，無一時之或怠焉；古人執事必有恪也，吾則恪敬於執事之際，無一事之敢慢焉。其敬之法於古人者又何如哉！夫樂既盛矣，敬既至矣，固是以感格先王之神矣，而湯孫之心尤不敢以是而自足也。謂夫成湯於冥冥之中，其庶幾顧我冬烝之祭乎？是祭也，乃湯孫所親奉，而非攝以他人也。烈祖於昭昭之際，其庶幾顧我秋嘗之祀乎？是祀也，乃湯孫所躬主，而非委之於他職也。拳拳焉致其丁寧之意，懇懇焉兾其眷顧之深，先王有不來格乎？抑是詩商人祀成湯而作也，然有樂焉必有禮，有禮焉必有樂。其所謂「庸鼓有斁，萬舞有奕」，則樂之和為可知；所謂「溫恭朝夕，執事有恪」，則禮之謹為可見。樂本於和，禮本於敬，此商人之禮樂所以為盛也歟！此其所以美盛德而告成功也歟！
translation_en:
… is handed down from antiquity; how fitting it is, then, that the people of Shang should hope for the fond regard of the former king! This ode is the music for sacrificing to Cheng Tang. Moreover, instruments of metal are called "large bells" (yong), and those of hide are called "drums" (gu); to say that they "resound" (you yi) means that their fast and slow tempos are regulated, and their clear and turbid tones complement one another, resounding in great splendor. Plumes and flutes are called "civil" (wen), and shields and battle-axes are called "martial" (wu) [?]; of the myriad dances (wanwu), to say that they are "grandly arrayed" (you yi) means that the dancing positions and boundaries are a sight to behold, and the ceremonial forms are unconfused, grandly arrayed in due order. Such is the magnificence of the music and dance that the descendants of previous dynasties, the guests assisting at the sacrifice, upon hearing the sound of the bells and drums, none fail to feel a sense of harmonious joy; and upon beholding the demeanor of the myriad dances, none fail to feel a heart of delighted pleasure. How great indeed is the power of music to move men!

Yet since the music moves men, how could reverence not be handed down from antiquity? Furthermore, it does not merely say "from antiquity" (zi gu), but must also say "in olden times" (zai xi), showing that the practice of this reverence did not belong to a single person; it does not merely say "in olden times," but must also say "among the former people" (xian min), showing that the practice of this reverence did not last for just a single day. The ancients were unfailingly mild and reverent morning and evening; we, too, are mild and reverent from morning to evening, without a single moment of laxity. The ancients, in conducting their duties, were unfailingly respectful; we, too, are respectfully attentive when conducting our duties, without a single affair in which we dare be negligent. How great, too, is our modeling of reverence upon the ancients!

Now, when the music is already so magnificent and the reverence already so utmost, it is certainly sufficient to move and reach the spirit of the former king; yet the heart of Tang's descendant still dares not be self-satisfied with this. He says: "Will Cheng Tang, in the unseen realm, perhaps look with favor upon our winter sacrifice (zheng)?" This sacrifice is personally offered by Tang's descendant, not performed by proxy through another. "Will the Illustrious Ancestor, in the bright realm above, perhaps look with favor upon our autumn sacrifice (chang)?" This sacrifice is personally presided over by Tang's descendant, not delegated to another office. Earnestly he conveys his repeated entreaties, and sincerely he hopes for the depth of his fond regard—how could the former king not come and be present?

After all, this ode was composed by the people of Shang for sacrificing to Cheng Tang. Yet where there is music, there must be ritual; and where there is ritual, there must be music. From what it calls "The large bells and drums resound; the myriad dances are grandly arrayed," the harmony of the music can be known; from what it calls "Mild and reverent morning and evening, conducting duties with respect," the carefulness of the ritual can be seen. Music is rooted in harmony, and ritual is rooted in reverence—is this not why the ritual and music of the people of Shang were so flourishing? And is this not how they praised flourishing virtue and announced accomplished success?

title: 景泰四年福建鄉試錄
text:
春秋義
齊高子來盟〔閔公二年〕楚屈完來盟于師〔僖公四年〕宋司馬華
孫來盟〔文公十五年〕
陳卿
同考試官訓導彭批此題作者往往失旨獨此篇詞嚴義
正超出衆作非深於屬辭此事之教者
不能也宜冠本經
考試官學正楊批經旨詳明允如初考
考試官教諭聶批來盟一也而予奪不同此篇乃見作
手宜冠本經
===
春秋予大夫得奉使之宜而不予大夫遂私交之好此司馬華孫之來所
所以不可與高子屈完而例論也春秋同以來盟書之而予奪存乎事
焉且夫古者人臣出境有可以安社稷利國家則專之可也今也高子
以齊之大夫閔公二年慶父稔惡魯國曠年無君齊桓遣高子至魯
以覘國之虛實非有安危継絶一定之計也屈完以楚之大夫僖公
四年齊桓伐楚八國同次于陘楚成使屈完如師以觀齊之強弱初
無請盟服義不易之命也然高子至不以兼國廣地為心惟以平
難善隣為美而僖公之位以定屈完來不恃方城漢水之險諾夫
punctuated:
《春秋》義

「齊高子來盟。」〔閔公二年〕「楚屈完來盟于師。」〔僖公四年〕「宋司馬華孫來盟。」〔文公十五年〕

陳卿

同考試官訓導彭批：此題作者往往失旨，獨此篇詞嚴義正，超出衆作。非深於屬辭此事之教者不能也，宜冠本經。
考試官學正楊批：經旨詳明，允如初考。
考試官教諭聶批：來盟一也，而予奪不同，此篇乃見作手，宜冠本經。

《春秋》予大夫得奉使之宜，而不予大夫遂私交之好，此司馬華孫之來，所所以不可與高子、屈完而例論也。《春秋》同以「來盟」書之，而予奪存乎事焉。且夫古者人臣出境，有可以安社稷、利國家，則專之可也。今也，高子以齊之大夫，閔公二年，慶父稔惡，魯國曠年無君，齊桓遣高子至魯，以覘國之虛實，非有安危継絶一定之計也。屈完以楚之大夫，僖公四年，齊桓伐楚，八國同次于陘，楚成使屈完如師，以觀齊之強弱，初無請盟服義不易之命也。然高子至，不以兼國廣地為心，惟以平難善隣為美，而僖公之位以定；屈完來，不恃方城、漢水之險，諾夫
translation_en:
Essay on the Spring and Autumn Annals (Chunqiu)

"Master Gao of Qi came to make a covenant." [Second year of Duke Min] "Qu Wan of Chu came to make a covenant with the army." [Fourth year of Duke Xi] "Hua Sun, Marshal of Song, came to make a covenant." [Fifteenth year of Duke Wen]

Chen Qing 陳卿

Comment by Associate Examiner and Assistant Instructor Peng 彭: Writers on this topic often miss the purport, yet this essay alone is strict in diction and upright in meaning, surpassing all the other compositions. Only one deeply versed in the teaching of "linking words and arranging events" in the Annals could have produced it. It ought to stand first in this Classic.
Comment by Examiner and Subprefectural Director of Studies Yang 楊: The purport of the Classic is expounded in full and clear detail; I concur with the initial evaluation.
Comment by Examiner and County Director of Studies Nie 聶: Their "coming to make a covenant" is the same, yet the praise and blame differ. This essay truly shows the hand of a master and ought to stand first in this Classic.

The Spring and Autumn Annals praises great officers for achieving what is appropriate in carrying out a mission, and does not praise great officers for pursuing the amity of private intercourse. This is why the coming of Marshal Hua Sun Hua Sun 華孫 cannot be discussed on the same footing as that of Master Gao Gaozi 高子 and Qu Wan 屈完. Although the Spring and Autumn Annals records all of them alike as "coming to make a covenant," the praise and blame reside in the events themselves. Now in antiquity, once a subject had crossed the border of his state, if there was something by which he could bring peace to the altars of soil and grain and benefit the state, he was permitted to act on his own authority. Consider the present cases: Master Gao was a great officer of Qi. In the second year of Duke Min, when Qingfu's 慶父 wickedness had ripened and the state of Lu had been without a ruler for a full year, Duke Huan of Qi 齊桓 dispatched Master Gao to Lu to spy out the strength and weakness of the state; he did not have a fixed plan to settle its crisis and restore its broken line. Qu Wan was a great officer of Chu. In the fourth year of Duke Xi, when Duke Huan of Qi attacked Chu and the eight states halted together at Xing 陘, King Cheng of Chu 楚成 sent Qu Wan to the army to observe the strength and weakness of Qi; at the outset he had no unalterable command to request a covenant and submit to righteousness. Yet when Master Gao arrived, he did not set his mind on annexing the state and expanding territory, but regarded only quelling disaster and befriending a neighbor as admirable, and thus the position of Duke Xi 僖公 was settled; when Qu Wan came, he did not rely on the natural barriers of the Fangcheng 方城 mountains and the Han River 漢水, but assented to…

title: 景泰四年福建鄉試錄
text:
徵與同好之言而召陵之禮以成盟出於已而無專制之嫌事適乎宜
而得出疆之義春秋於二子之來皆不稱使所以予其得奉使之宜也為何
如若夫人臣義無私交大夫非君命不越境乃禮制之常也今也華孫
以司馬之官世秉宋國之政不輔其君以弭穆襄之禍謀自免討私為
盟魯之舉敢專君謀禮非不恭也而非利國家之謀承命亞旅詞
非不善也而非安社稷之計其來也樹黨與以自固而國君不聞其盟
也結隣好以自安而君命未請無君之心以兆不臣之念以長比之高子
之盟固倍蓰之相遠矣較諸屈完之來又豈徑庭之可侔哉春秋於
華孫之來不稱使者所以著其私交之罪也又何如吁三子之得失不
===
同春秋之書法則一所謂美惡不嫌於同詞見矣大抵春秋一經之中來
盟不稱使者三而華孫之來固不足論矣然高子今日之安魯固可
美矣而前日于防之盟魯未免有抗尊之失屈完今日之服齊固可
嘉矣而後日楚人之滅黃未嘗有格君之善合而觀之思過半矣
公會晉侯齊侯宋公蔡侯鄭伯衛子莒子盟于踐土僖公二十八年
同盟于亳城北襄公十一年
陳廷玉
同考試官訓導彭批此題本平易而作者多戾經旨惟此篇文
理通暢深合題意故表而出之
punctuated:
徵與同好之言，而召陵之禮以成。盟出於已，而無專制之嫌；事適乎宜，而得出疆之義。《春秋》於二子之來，皆不稱「使」，所以予其得奉使之宜也為何如！若夫人臣義無私交，大夫非君命不越境，乃禮制之常也。今也，華孫以司馬之官，世秉宋國之政，不輔其君以弭穆、襄之禍，謀自免討，私為盟魯之舉，敢專君謀。禮非不恭也，而非利國家之謀；承命亞旅，詞非不善也，而非安社稷之計。其來也，樹黨與以自固，而國君不聞；其盟也，結隣好以自安，而君命未請。無君之心以兆，不臣之念以長。比之高子之盟，固倍蓰之相遠矣；較諸屈完之來，又豈徑庭之可侔哉！《春秋》於華孫之來不稱「使」者，所以著其私交之罪也，又何如！吁，三子之得失不同，《春秋》之書法則一，所謂「美惡不嫌於同詞」見矣。大抵《春秋》一經之中，來盟不稱「使」者三，而華孫之來固不足論矣。然高子今日之安魯，固可美矣，而前日于防之盟魯，未免有抗尊之失；屈完今日之服齊，固可嘉矣，而後日楚人之滅黃，未嘗有格君之善。合而觀之，思過半矣。

公會晉侯、齊侯、宋公、蔡侯、鄭伯、衛子、莒子盟于踐土（僖公二十八年）；同盟于亳城北（襄公十一年）。

陳廷玉

同考試官訓導彭批：此題本平易，而作者多戾經旨。惟此篇文理通暢，深合題意，故表而出之。
translation_en:
… words concerning the failure of tribute and the sharing of amity, and thus the ritual at Shaoling was accomplished. The covenants originated from themselves, yet they incurred no suspicion of acting arbitrarily; their actions suited what was appropriate, and thus they fulfilled the righteous duty of an envoy who has crossed the border. With regard to the arrival of these two men, the Spring and Autumn Annals (Chunqiu) in neither case designates them as "sent as envoy" (shi)—how great indeed is its approval of their having attained what was appropriate in carrying out a mission!

As for the principle that a subject in his righteous duty has no private foreign relations, and that a Grand Master does not cross the border without his ruler's command—this is the constant norm of ritual institutions. Now, however, Hua Sun, holding the office of Minister of War (Sima) and hereditarily wielding the government of the state of Song, did not assist his ruler to quell the calamities of the clans of Mu and Xiang; instead, scheming to save himself from punishment, he privately undertook the act of making a covenant with Lu, daring to usurp his ruler's counsels. His ritual demeanor was not unrespectful, yet it was no plan to benefit the state; his requesting to receive commands only from the secondary officials (yalü) was not unskillful in phrasing, yet it was no policy to stabilize the altars of soil and grain. In coming, he established factional partisans to secure himself, while his ruler knew nothing of it; in covenanting, he contracted neighborly amity to keep himself safe, without having requested his ruler's command. A heart disregardful of his ruler was thereby portended, and unministerial intentions thereby grew. Compared to the covenant of Gaozi, it is certainly fivefold removed in distance; measured against the coming of Qu Wan, how could the disparity be merely that of a courtyard and a passageway! That the Spring and Autumn Annals does not designate Hua Sun as "sent as envoy" upon his arrival is the means by which it makes manifest his crime of engaging in private foreign relations—how severe indeed!

Alas! The merits and faults of these three men are different, yet the historiographical principle of the Spring and Autumn Annals is one and the same; what is meant by "not shrinking from using identical phrasing for both the admirable and the wicked" is here seen. Broadly speaking, throughout the entire Classic of the Spring and Autumn Annals, there are three instances of someone coming to make a covenant without being designated "sent as envoy," and the coming of Hua Sun is certainly not even worth discussing. Yet while Gaozi's stabilizing of Lu on this day is indeed admirable, on a previous day, when魯 covenanted at Fang, there was unavoidably the fault of defying a superior; and while Qu Wan's submission to Qi on this day is indeed praiseworthy, on a later day, when the men of Chu destroyed Huang, he never had the merit of rectifying his ruler. If one views them together, more than half will be understood.

"The Duke met the Marquis of Jin, the Marquis of Qi, the Duke of Song, the Marquis of Cai, the Earl of Zheng, the Heir of Wei, and the Viscount of Ju, and made a covenant at Jiantu" (28th year of Duke Xi); "[The Duke and the lords] together made a covenant north of the city of Bo" (11th year of Duke Xiang).

Chen Tingyu

Comment (pi) by Associate Examiner and Confucian School Assistant Instructor (Xundao) Peng: This topic is inherently straightforward, yet most examinees ran counter to the purport of the Classic. Only this essay is fluent in both style and reasoning and deeply accords with the meaning of the topic; therefore, we have singled it out for publication.

title: 景泰四年福建鄉試錄
text:
考試官學正揚批文暢理明初考取之當也
考試官教諭聶批二公皆獎王室春秋所嘉此篇深
合本旨宜在選列
繼覇者講信以獎王室固可美復覇者講信以獎王室亦可嘉此文
悼之尊王春秋得不備書而並予之哉且夫踐土之盟果何盟乎盖晋文
獎王而有是舉也于斯之時因天王之下勞合列國以講好獻俘衡雍而
昭敵愾之功要言王庭而伸尊獎之誠展夫出入三覲之敬致夫天威
咫尺之恭水木本源之油然而興江漢朝宗之義藹然而著則晋文獎
王之功為何如耶若夫亳北之盟又何盟乎盖晋悼獎王而有是役也
===
當是之時因鄭人之行成率諸侯以同歃大侯小伯咸知以獎王為
心友邦冢君皆知以獎王為務尊周室於旣卑之時收人心於渙
散之際上天下澤之分由是而明衣裳冠冕之念由是而起則晋悼獎
王之義又何如耶吁即踐土之盟于以見晋文獎王之功顯即亳北之盟
于以見晋悼獎王之義著春秋備書而並予之意昭昭矣雖然論
覇者之功不可不論其過晋文今日踐土之獎王固可美矣然後日會
于溫而請王出狩盟翟泉而上替下陵又豈可美乎晋悼今日亳北
之獎王亦可嘉矣然前日盟雞澤而瀆慢王臣會邢丘而委政大夫
又豈可嘉乎讀經者得不有慨於斯
punctuated:
考試官學正揚批：文暢理明，初考取之當也。
考試官教諭聶批：二公皆獎王室，《春秋》所嘉。此篇深合本旨，宜在選列。
繼覇者講信以獎王室，固可美；復覇者講信以獎王室，亦可嘉。此文、悼之尊王，《春秋》得不備書而並予之哉？且夫踐土之盟，果何盟乎？盖晋文獎王而有是舉也。于斯之時，因天王之下勞，合列國以講好。獻俘衡雍，而昭敵愾之功；要言王庭，而伸尊獎之誠。展夫出入三覲之敬，致夫天威咫尺之恭。水木本源之油然而興，江漢朝宗之義藹然而著，則晋文獎王之功為何如耶？若夫亳北之盟，又何盟乎？盖晋悼獎王而有是役也。當是之時，因鄭人之行成，率諸侯以同歃。大侯小伯，咸知以獎王為心；友邦冢君，皆知以獎王為務。尊周室於旣卑之時，收人心於渙散之際。上天下澤之分由是而明，衣裳冠冕之念由是而起，則晋悼獎王之義又何如耶？吁！即踐土之盟，于以見晋文獎王之功顯；即亳北之盟，于以見晋悼獎王之義著。《春秋》備書而並予之意，昭昭矣。雖然，論覇者之功，不可不論其過。晋文今日踐土之獎王，固可美矣；然後日會于溫而請王出狩，盟翟泉而上替下陵，又豈可美乎？晋悼今日亳北之獎王，亦可嘉矣；然前日盟雞澤而瀆慢王臣，會邢丘而委政大夫，又豈可嘉乎？讀經者得不有慨於斯！
translation_en:
Examiner and Subprefectural Instructor (xuezheng) Yang [?] comments: The prose flows smoothly and the reasoning is clear; its selection in the initial review was well justified.

Examiner and County Instructor (jiaoyu) Nie comments: Both dukes supported the royal house, which the Spring and Autumn Annals (Chunqiu) commends. This essay deeply accords with the fundamental purport and deserves to be placed among the selected essays.

When one who succeeds to the hegemony cultivates good faith in order to support the royal house, it is certainly admirable; when one who restores the hegemony cultivates good faith in order to support the royal house, it is likewise commendable. Regarding this honoring of the king by Dukes Wen and Dao of Jin, how could the Spring and Autumn Annals not record both in full and grant approval to them alike?

Now then, what covenant was the covenant at Jiantu? It was an action undertaken because Duke Wen of Jin was supporting the king. At that time, occasioned by the Heavenly King's coming down to reward his troops, he brought together the various states to cultivate friendly relations. Presenting captives at Hengyong, he made manifest his achievement in withstanding the king's enemies; plighting his word in the royal court, he expressed his sincerity in honoring and supporting the throne. He displayed the reverence of having three audiences upon entering and departing, and showed the deference due to the royal majesty at close quarters. The sentiment of water and trees having their source and root arose spontaneously, and the righteousness of the Jiang and Han rivers paying court to the sea became abundantly manifest—how great, then, was Duke Wen of Jin's merit in supporting the king!

And what covenant, again, was the covenant north of Bo? It was a campaign undertaken because Duke Dao of Jin was supporting the king. At that time, occasioned by the people of Zheng suing for peace, he led the feudal lords to smear their lips with blood together in a common oath. Great marquises and lesser earls all knew to take supporting the king as their mind; the rulers of friendly states all knew to take supporting the king as their duty. He honored the House of Zhou at a time when it had already fallen low, and gathered back men's allegiances at a moment when they had become scattered. The distinction between heaven above and the marsh below was thereby made clear, and loyalty to the ceremonial robes and crowns of the royal order was thereby aroused—how great, again, was Duke Dao of Jin's righteousness in supporting the king!

Alas! From the covenant at Jiantu one sees the splendor of Duke Wen of Jin's merit in supporting the king; from the covenant north of Bo one sees the prominence of Duke Dao of Jin's righteousness in supporting the king. The intention of the Spring and Autumn Annals in recording both in full and approving them together is crystal clear!

Even so, in discussing the merits of hegemons, one cannot fail to discuss their faults as well. Duke Wen of Jin's supporting the king today at Jiantu was certainly admirable; yet later, when he met at Wen and summoned the king to go out on a royal hunt, and when he covenanted at Diquan where superiors were disregarded and inferiors encroached upon their betters, how could that be called admirable? Duke Dao of Jin's supporting the king today north of Bo was likewise commendable; yet earlier, when he covenanted at Jize and treated the king's minister with disrespect, and when he met at Xingqiu and delegated state governance to the great officers, how could that be called commendable? How can readers of the Classic not sigh over this!

title: 景泰四年福建鄉試錄
text:
禮記義
仁者仁此者也禮者履此者也義者宜此者也信者信此者也強
者強此者也
鄧珙
同考試官教諭黎批此篇之作雅而不浮澹而有味必熟
於禮者一薦奚忝
考試官學正楊批發明衆德成孝之理極是宜登選列
考試官教諭聶批無冗長之詞有簡澹之味初考得之
高薦宜矣
===
德具於人雖殊德施於孝則一夫孝之行雖大必資衆德以成之也使
人之德有一而不施於孝又何以盡事親之道哉見於祭義之篇其旨如
此今夫在人之行莫大於事親之孝孝行之成必由於衆德之資是故
仁主於愛愛莫大於愛親人能盡其愛親之心則仁之施不失其序然
仁非先施於孝豈得謂仁之德乎禮主於敬敬莫先於敬親人能行
其敬親之禮則禮之用必踐其實然禮非能履於孝豈得謂禮之德
乎至若合宜之謂義茍不順其理之當然而陷親於不義則義之德
必虧是義也者不過宜於孝而已以實之謂信茍不能實矣其心之所
發而事親以不誠則信之德必妄是信也者不過實於孝而已然曰仁
punctuated:
禮記義

「仁者，仁此者也；禮者，履此者也；義者，宜此者也；信者，信此者也；強者，強此者也。」

鄧珙

同考試官教諭黎批：此篇之作，雅而不浮，澹而有味，必熟於《禮》者，一薦奚忝？
考試官學正楊批：發明衆德成孝之理極是，宜登選列。
考試官教諭聶批：無冗長之詞，有簡澹之味，初考得之，高薦宜矣。

德具於人雖殊，德施於孝則一。夫孝之行雖大，必資衆德以成之也。使人之德有一而不施於孝，又何以盡事親之道哉？見於《祭義》之篇，其旨如此。今夫在人之行，莫大於事親之孝；孝行之成，必由於衆德之資。是故仁主於愛，愛莫大於愛親。人能盡其愛親之心，則仁之施不失其序。然仁非先施於孝，豈得謂仁之德乎？禮主於敬，敬莫先於敬親。人能行其敬親之禮，則禮之用必踐其實。然禮非能履於孝，豈得謂禮之德乎？至若合宜之謂義，茍不順其理之當然而陷親於不義，則義之德必虧；是義也者，不過宜於孝而已。以實之謂信，茍不能實矣其心之所發而事親以不誠，則信之德必妄；是信也者，不過實於孝而已。然曰仁、
translation_en:
Expositions on the Record of Rites (Liji)

"Benevolence means acting benevolently toward this; ritual propriety means putting this into practice; righteousness means acting appropriately toward this; trustworthiness means being true to this; and moral strength means exerting oneself in this."

Deng Gong

Associate Examiner and County Director of Studies (jiaoyu) Li comments: The composition of this essay is refined without being superficial, and understated yet rich in flavor. He must be someone thoroughly versed in the Rites; what shame could there be in recommending him?
Examiner and Subprefectural Director of Studies (xuezheng) Yang comments: It elucidates the principle of how the various virtues bring filial piety to completion most aptly; he deserves to ascend to the ranks of the selected.
Examiner and County Director of Studies (jiaoyu) Nie comments: Free of verbose phrasing and possessing a concise, understated flavor—having obtained this in the initial reading, a high recommendation is well deserved.

Although the virtues endowed in human beings differ, in their application to filial piety they are one. Now, great though the practice of filial piety is, it must rely upon the various virtues to be brought to completion. Suppose there were even one among a person's virtues not applied to filial piety—how then could one fully realize the way of serving one's parents? As seen in the chapter "The Meaning of Sacrifices" (Jiyi), such is its purport. Now, among human conduct, nothing is greater than the filial piety of serving one's parents; and the completion of filial conduct must come from reliance upon the various virtues.
